subsubtopic: HOLMES FOUNDRY COMPANY, SARNIA, ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) to a very grave situation which exists in Sarnia. The Holmes Foundry Company, which is controlled by Port Huron, Michigan interests, is located in Sarnia. It seems that the workers in this foundry have gone on strike demanding what workers in the United States have already received. These men were attacked, the union organizer in particular, by a mob, the attack being carried into the homes of the men. I should like to ask whether the Minister of Labour proposes to make an independent inquiry concerning this matter.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, this matter was brought to my attention yesterday by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray). I assured him that if the Department of Labour could be of service in the matter it would be pleased indeed to send a conciliation officer to Sarnia. I believe the matter is now under consideration by the mayor of Sarnia, in so far as it still calls for intervention or conciliation. My latest information, however, is that the dispute as such has been settled. So far as any property damage is concerned, I take it that this will be a matter for the provincial authorities.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned yesterday I was endeavouring to point out that both this year and last year this group had at least endeavoured to indicate the direction in which we had to go to bring about economic security and to banish from our midst not so much unemployment as destitution. I have wondered many times whether ministers of the crown have ever taken the trouble or have been sufficiently interested to go to some, of the relief camps of western Canada or to the soup kitchens throughout the country to see for themselves the terrible price we are paying because of our apathy in respect to this question.
I believe the first duty of a government is to look after its people, and all other things must take a secondary place. That is the responsibility of the present Liberal government. Both this and the last government failed miserably to bring about a happy life for Canadian people who are unemployed!. We speak of everything in terms of dollars and cents. We always measure cost in money, and many statements made in the house have been contradictory. For instance, we have been told that prosperity is returning. I would suggest to the government that the unemployed' in Canada are not sharing in that prosperity. If there is any section of Canadian society which has paid the price of the deflationary period through which we have passed, it is the unemployed. To-day I want to make a plea for those whose hopes have been frustrated and who, through the years, have been waiting for a generous government to do something for them. I should like to ask the government to state its long range view on the question. Are we waiting for increasing external trade? Is that the only hope for Canadian youth? Are we waiting until such time as we may have a greater volume of trade before these people can be absorbed into industry and can obtain economic security? If we are, then I say now to the government that for these people there is no hope.
As I said last night, in the last six years we have spent over a billion dollars on relief, and the position of the unemployed in Canada is no better to-day than it was four or five years ago. I see no hope in expanding trade. I do not believe it is natural, even,-and while there have been some expressions in the house regarding increases in prices of farm products and increases in volume of production, we must remember that we are now entering an inflationary period. The demand for Canadian products in the markets of the world does not arise because the people of Europe are consuming more; it is not a natural demand. So far as Canada is concerned, our greatest market is the Canadian market, and if we are to bring economic security to these people, if we are to give them a greater measure of hope and an opportunity for creative life, then I say to the government there is only one way it can be done.
This little group has endeavoured to point out time and time again-and through the years we will still hammer at this one thing, something the government absolutely refuses to touch-that there must be monetary reform. The wage system has broken down. It is unscientific; it is unsound; it does not give the great masses of the people that opportunity and that security which our production and our scientific knowledge have made available to us. After all, what is the purpose of an economic system? How do we measure prosperity? Do we measure it by the increased profits of great industries? I do not think so. The standard of living of the Canadian people should be measured in one way, and in one only, and that is the making of their lives secure to a point commensurate with the ability of the Canadian people to produce goods.
A few days ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) made a statement to the effect that purchasing power comes from production. I challenge that statement. Purchasing power does not come from production. Production is one thing; the monetary system is another. In Canada we have the ability to produce great volumes of wealth. We have the machinery; we are a generation better equipped than any which has preceded us, and still we find unfortunate people passing through the years without a break. I make a plea for the unemployed in Canada: for God's sake let us get down to business! Let us get these people through the present transitional period, through this time of great change, and give them a break. Give them an opportunity to live; give them something-some measure of hope. We must not be content
The Budget-Mr. Poole

with fooling around, dilly-dallying, doing nothing, waiting for expanding trade, or hoping for something to fall from heaven which will help us out.
I said last night, and I now repeat, that the volume of international trade will be less, not more, in years to come. Every nation is becoming self-sufficient. The foundation and basis of the system under which we are living to-day is the ability of nations to export greater volume of goods. As each nation becomes self-sufficient there will be a lesser demand for Canadian products. In terms of the capitalistic system, under which we live, it will mean that there will be less wages paid. As each nation becomes selfsufficient, irrespective of our great wealth, our natural resources and our production through machine and scientific skill, the lots of the great masses of the people will become more miserable and the debts of nations will rise.
I am sure many hon. members do not understand what it means to go on drifting through the years. Men who are married and with families, but without jobs, know none of the natural pleasures or luxuries of life; in many cases, they have not even the necessities. We have set up a commission; there have been suggestions here and suggestions there, but we have not yet got to the root of this problem, and there has not been a suggestion in this house as to what is the real cause of destitution. Let us at this session do something definite to help the unemployed people of Canada-not with charitable doles, but, until such time as this government has monetary reform thrust upon it, let it be recognized that wages is the only medium whereby these men can receive the necessities of life; so for God's sake let us give them wages. We need roads, we need houses; there is in this country fifty years' work to be done. We have great production and on the other hand great poverty. I ask the government now to get down to the root of this matter, not to leave it until next year or the year afterwards as material for another election promise. Let us construct a better Canada, recognizing that our most valuable asset is the youth of the country, now better equipped than youth has ever been before; let us not be always measuring this problem by considerations of dollars and cents. After all, money is only a ticket; it is an expedient by which we distribute goods and services. We have the goods, the services, the machines, the natural resources. Let us give the young people of Canada happiness, security, a future, and a more creative life than they have known in the last six years.

This is the greatest responsibility before the government to-day; in comparison with it all other things fall into insignificance, because by continuing as we are doing we destroy the souls of human beings and condemn them to live without hope, without objective, without a future. That is the penalty we pay for measuring this problem in terms of dollars and cents. The greatest cost of the depression can never be computed in that way; for it is a moral loss, a tragedy of lost hopes and lost opportunities. That is the history of the generation to which I belong. To that generation this government it responsible; to that generation it will have to answer some day. The question cannot be thrust lightly aside; it will remain with us even though the government tries to forget about it. What we sow to-day we shall reap to-morrow. If therefore as Canadians we are interested in building up this country, let us remember that our greatest asset is the youth of Canada, and that we are responsible for giving them opportunities to live creative lives.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is not in his seat this afternoon. I regret also to hear that illness keeps him away, for he is one who commands the respect and admiration of every hon. member of this house and of the country at large. A short time ago I lived around the corner from him in Rosedale. At that time he was not a member of this house, from 1930 to 1935, but I well remember the tribute which he, as a private citizen of this country, paid to my leader, who was then bearing great burdens as the prime minister of this country. The Minister of Finance may not thereby have won applause from his own party or from the political machine of his party, but he won the admiration and respect of all right-thinking citizens, including a great newspaperman, the late Harry Anderson, chief editor of the Toronto Globe. The minister (Mr. Dunning) referred at that time to the absolute necessity of every good citizen coming to the support of the government of the day in the great crisis-the greatest depression the world has even seen-that then confronted the country. I am glad to pay him this tribute as a great Canadian then, and as a patriot. I am thankful that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who was then shouldering greater burdens than even the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier or Sir John A. Macdonald had to face, has regained his health, and I

The Budget-Mr. Church
believe he will rank very high in. the history of this country, as he does with all the members of this house.
In this connection I might refer to the remarks of another member of the govern-, ment, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), who is either not in his seat this afternoon or has gone out: I would rather have said in his presence what I have to say. I have nothing against him personally. A month ago, and again on Tuesday evening, he alluded to the leader of the opposition, who has been giving the government of the day the best of support, in accordance with a good British principle; because he realizes that, while we are in opposition to hon. gentlemen opposite, they are a government of Canadians and will do what they no doubt believe to be the best not only for their own party but for the general good of the country.	I myself am not a very strong or
bigoted party man; neither is the leader of the opposition, because he is a great empire statesman on the British model. In this budget the Minister of Finance is simply carrying out, with some reductions, modifications and some extensions and deductions, the great British Empire agreement that was made in 1932, by my hon. leader and but for which the depression and unemployment would have been ten times worse than they are to-day. I was glad to notice that Mr. Joseph Atkinson of the Toronto Star has in an article in the Star by Observer paid tribute to Mr. Bennett. The bouquets which my right hon. leader received from the Minister of Labour are gratefully accepted, both those of a month ago and those on Tuesday evening, andi acknowledged on this side. But the minister delivered a moral lecture to the unemployed and to private members and to the opposition, and I may remind him that, although he is a professor, we do not need any lectures from him on unemployment. In the olden days it used to be said that "an apple a day keeps the doctor away." Now, with the Minister of Labour, it seems that a professor a day keeps the bailiff away. Last Tuesday night the Minister of Labour referred to the right hon. leader of the opposition and used the words:
In spite of flagrant distortion and misunderstanding with regard to the attitude of the Labour department.
There appeared on February 11 of this year in the Toronto Star, a Liberal organ, an idea too great for mere party politics: in a whole double header column "The Observer'' pays tribute to the right hon. the 31111-93
leader of the opposition and says he is assured of a distinguished place in Canadian history. I quote:
No single act in his long and notable political career will be so long and so gratefully remembered by posterity as his proposal in the House of Commons last Monday evening that the dominion government should go into the business of gold mining.
The writer goes on to refer to all he has done in his many years of public service and the principles for which he stood during the five years that he was Prime Minister. He mentions the resources of the country.
Riches, once remarked the prince of American preachers, are like manure. Heaped in one small spot it is a noisome and unwholesome mass; distributed over the whole field it means fertility and beauty and plenty.
This tribute, paid to my leader by a Liberal paper, is well deserved, because he has in this parliament again proved himself a statesman. He has given the government independent support when he believed it to be justified, and he deserves all credit for the empire trade agreements of 1932, which saved this country from bankruptcy, notwithstanding the opinions of the Minister of Labour, who at that time was not a member of this house. In so doing, the former prime minister and the present Minister of Finance have revived the policies of the late Joseph Chamberlain on tariff reform and preferential trade with the dominions and our best customer the mother land. Our leader started it, and what we have now is a vest pocket edition of it with a few cuts here and there. As Canadians let us not forget the lessons of history. For every dollar we put into the pockets of John Bull he pays us back ten times over. I do not know where our industries and the prairies would be without the British market; it is the most steadfast market we have and not one here to-day and gone to-morrow. As regards the great questions of trade, defence and immigration, let us learn from Australia and New Zealand and keep Canada a white man's country.
Last July, in the great city of Birmingham, which for two generations has led all the cities in the empire as a well-governed city, they celebrated the anniversary of the birth of Joseph Chamberlain. Where is the man anywhere who did for his city what Chamberlain did while mayor of Birmingham? Although he was bora in London, he gave away for the benefit of his city the fortune he made. He was without doubt one of the greatest Englishmen, if not the greatest, of the nineteenth century.

The Budget-Mr. Church

Chamberlain's vision was one of the glories of the Victorian and Edwardian eras, both at home and abroad. Britain took thirty years to find out that he was right on the tariff, at great cost to her people and to the working classes, and to the welfare of her dominions. Kipling's tribute to him was written in 1904, two years before his great policy was rejected, in which the poet says:
Thrones, powers, dominions block the view With episodes and underlings,
The meek historian deems them true,
Nor heeds the song that Clio sings-
The simple, central truth that stings The mob to boo, the priest to ban.
(Things never yet created things).
Once on a time there was a man.
And under that man British statecraft and diplomacy reached their greatest heights of all time. He was too big for the smallness of the House of Commons which under our so-called democracy is fast becoming a mock parliament. If the tariff policy proposed by Chamberlain in 1906 had been adopted I doubt whether there would have been a world war.
And now I wish to say a few words with regard to the policies of the Minister of Labour. About a year ago he delivered a series of lectures in this house, all purely theoretical -because if ever there was a theorist he is one. He is not a practical administrator of public affairs. As I say, about a year ago he delivered certain lectures in which he quoted copiously from the pages of Carlyle. May day was approaching, and if he had handed the unemployed a bound copy of Carlyle it would have been just as effective as anything practical that he did. There were as many out of work. Well, I have a copy of a work dealing with: the du Pont dynasty written, by John K. Winkler of New York, and reference is made to the head of the commission. This gentleman, is the head of the du Pont dynasty in this	country-gentlemen who made
hundreds of millions of dollars out of the war and got away with it, subject to no regulation. The senate of the United States has been showing what this particular concern has been doing.
I want to say something with regard' to the minister's policy, because a year ago I took strong ground against a commission being appointed on behalf of the unemployed. But a commission was appointed, and the large staff whom Mr. Purvis engaged to work on that commission, if they stood two deep, would extend from here to the Chateau Laurier. These are the people who are appointed to work on this useless commission. Mr. Purvis said that he wanted to get the facts. The municipalities already had all

the facts; for we know to-day, just as we knew then, how many registered1 unemployed there are in the various cities of Canada. The city relief departments could all have given him the information he wanted, but he adopted a system of registration of his own for Canada that was not accurate. This commission does not know half the unemployed in the riding I represent. I say that because there are a number of the unemployed who are not on relief. Many of them are near the point of starvation, but these men, good honest industrial workers, are too proud to take relief and consequently are suffering untold hardship.
I have always thought that one of the cardinal principles of Liberalism was the right to deputize, but the minister has denied that right, because a deputation of the corporation from Toronto was refused a hearing by the Minister of Labour. They saw a courtly gentleman, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who was acting prime minister last fall, and he received quite courteously the mayor and board of control of that city. He listened attentively to them and replied that when the Prime Minister came back he would lay before him the representations that had been submitted by this deputation. But what did the Minister of Labour do, this new disciple of Liberalism? He simply told the mayor and board of control that he would not receive them, advising them instead to go and see Mr. Purvis, the representative in Canada of the du Pont dynasty, president of the Dunlop company, and director of the Bell Telephone company, the Bank of Montreal, the Sun Life, Chemical Industries and General Motors of New York. The deputation was informed that it might be allowed to see this citizen, and this in face of the fact that outside labour had been brought into the country in contravention of the alien labour act. In some of our industries-there was one in my riding-Americans were put to work, having been brought in in violation of that act. What about the right to deputize? I remember the time long ago-it is one of my earliest memories-when as a member of the city council I came down with a deputation as president of the Union of Canadian Municipalities representing the municipalities to interview Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We were received most courteously by Sir Wilfrid. He waited patiently until every member of the delegation was seated before he would allow us to proceed with the business that had brought us to Ottawa, and he gave us a patient hearing.

The Budget-Mr. Church
I asked a question the other day in this house but I got no answer. The Minister of Labour has compelled the municipalities to go hat in hand to this useless national employment commission which came into being on the first of April last-an appropriate day for such an event. But the unemployed got nothing out of it; there were no jobs to be had. This commission has ignored entirely the industrial workers of Canada, constituting fifty per cent of the population. I have here a return laid on the table by the Minister of Labour on February 15, 1937, showing how the municipalities of Quebec have been treated. I am not objecting to any benefits extended to that province, which contributes largely to the revenues of the country, but I find that in Quebec city provision has been made for parks, public baths, fences, public toilets, paving alleys in park, drains, water services and correlated works including material, the total estimated cost of all such construction being $100,000. In Three Rivers provision is made for the court house which is to be enlarged and improved; there are expenditures in LTslet, Sherbrooke and Wolfe; in Three Rivers there are to be various repairs and additions to St. Maurice river bridges, amounting to $160,000. and many other public works of a similar kind. There is a whole list here amounting to $2,750,000. When you come to Ontario what was done? This is a report tabled by the Minister of Labour on January 15, under the Unemployment Relief and Assistance Act, 1936. I pleaded with the minister last session to amend the act to give direct relief to the municipalities and enable him to enter into relief agreements with them, especially the larger municipalities, such as Toronto, Winnipeg, Montreal, Quebec, Vancouver and Hamilton. How much was the province of Ontario given? Not one red cent. The city of Toronto brought down a $4,000,000 relief works program; the revenue collected from there was $91,000,000, but Toronto never got a cent. When on September 16 last the government made an agreement with Ontario and gave them a large sum of money, how was it spent? On road's in new Ontario, roads in almost every Liberal constituency in that province. I have a list here; it is too long to read, but any hon. member can get this return, No. 115. Many of these roads are purely municipal undertakings, but the province was given all this money over the heads of the municipalities, which got nothing. All Toronto city got was $15,000 for some improvements in the post office, including two revolving doors, and one revolving door in the riding of the hon. member for Danforth
31111-93$
(Mr. Harris). Toronto had to contribute $125,000 for the island breakwater. It is the first time since confederation that the city of Toronto has been asked to contribute anything to it, and in my opinion it was very unwise to do so, because it is contrary to the British North America Act. The island is the breakwater for Toronto harbour and in other places the federal government pays all the cost.
I asked the Minister of Labour the question: what grants towards this relief to municipalities were made in Ontario by order in council? There has not been one order in council passed for those works, notwithstanding the money has been appropriated. I asked him in the house last Monday:
What municipal works in Ontario were so aided, giving the name of the municipality in Ontario in each case.
And his reply was, "Same as No. 1." That refers to an agreement with Ontario tabled January 15. It was not set out at all in that return; not one municipality or town got a dollar. That is the way the minister has treated the municipalities of this province, I very much regret that the municipalities of ' Ontario have been treated1 in the manner indicated. The report of the assessment commissioner of Toronto shows how home owners have been reduced under the depression. In 1929 home ownership in Toronto, according to the report of the assessment department, amounted to 63,417 out of 105,112 occupied dwellings, or sixty per cent. In 1936 the number had decreased to 59,093 out of a total of 108,065, less than fifty-five per cent. The assessment reports for 1935-36 indicate the extent to which the depression has made renters out of families which previously held an equity in the premises. The depression has forced two or three families into one house or apartment. This number was 3,407 in 1932 and in 1936 it is reduced to 2.129.
The Minister of Labour and the government have made a further raid on the municipalities. I am sorry the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) is not here. They passed an act in 1936. chapter 38, amending the Income War Tax Act, adding section 76A, under which the Minister of National Revenue collects income tax for the provincial governments. I thought the government were better politicians than to send out tax collectors and bailiffs to collect a duplicate income tax from the starved municipalities and force them to put it on real estate. The inebme tax was exclusively a prerogative of the municipalities from 1867 to 1918, when it was taken away by a duplicate income tax by the dominion for
The Budget-Mr. Church

war purposes. Now along comes the province and collects an income tax. The Minister of National Revenue has been making speeches in Ontario. If he had told them that he is the man who is collecting duplicate income tax and putting the bailiff in on them, he might have been telling something practical. That statute should be repealed; the municipalities should get their tax back. In the case of Toronto, 82,600.000 has been taken away; they have been given some back but the city is still out 8862,000, as a result of the new system and will have to add that loss to real estate.
I should like to find out from the Minister of Labour what plan the government has from now to the first of May to provide useful employment this spring for the great number of unemployed. Nothing is being done. The commission has no suburban policy. Half the people of this country are industrial workers. I have pleaded for them in this house before, asking some measure of protection to save their equity. What has the commission done for these poor workmen? Absolutely nothing. In Toronto and York west, north and east there is a. population of workmen who have been driven to the wall by the hard1 times, many of them on relief, and have lost their equity in that property. A great many are not on relief, because they are too independent, but they have lost their equity in their homes. What has the commission done for these men? Not a thing. In England they have done something, by balanced budgets, by tariffs, by sane and sensible housing and reconstruction policies, a safe suburban policy for the workers; and by state assistance to the industrial worker. They have had to tide them over bad times, as this parliament has the fishermen and the farmers. But this commission of figureheads has done nothing but make reports, and have forgotten all about the suburban and industrial worker. They have a youth committee now, and all they do is travel on the trains. They have made reports, and what are these reports? Mr. Burton of Simpson's wanted to have a regimentation of youth, a regular standing army. The Minister of Labour seems to have a small standing army in his department. In the United States one man, Mr. Hopkins, can handle all that work of relief for a population of 129,000,000, but this country's labour department is the most useless department of the government. It should be called the department of capital, not of labour. It is the most useless organization of any department in the government and I know something about labour conditions.

I see my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Spence) here. The government have not been altogether kind to him; they have amalgamated his Irish regiment with the Toronto Scottish. He is very popular with the industrial workers in his constituency, and he can see as a military man that an ordinary militia regiment is not to be compared with the Minister of Labour's unemployed commission regiment. Mr. Purvis is not a military man. He was bom in England, and a short time before the war started he went to the United States and then went down to South America. After the war he came to Montreal and became a millionaire as the representative of the du Pont and other interests. He has a small standing army of an unemployment commission all making reports. It consists of privates making reports under this act to the lance-corporal, the lance-corporal making reports to the corporal, the corporal to the lieutenant, the lieutenant to the captain, the captain to the major, the major to the colonel, and so on to the major-general, Mr. Purvis- a long retinue making reports before they reach the minister under the act. And while this is going on the industrial workers in my own and many other ridings have been driven out of their homes and have lost their equity, while waiting for this useless commission to do something. Is it any wonder that the right hon. leader of the opposition-notwithstanding the great assistance that he has given this government, supporting things which he deemed it to be the duty of the opposition to support-used the language he did in this house? I am prepared to use language ten times stronger, if necessary, for I know and have seen something about these conditions.
In my riding there are families whose great grandfathers, whose grandfathers and whose fathers owned property. Now many of the sons are industrial workers, many of their children are out of work and some of them are on relief. What has happened? The oldest boys do not like to hang around the house when they are not able to earn anything, so they take to the rods and wander looking for work as far as British 'Columbia. I saw some of these young fellows last summer; I found nearly sixty-five of them riding the box cars. The train was halted and I got out of my automobile and started talking to some of them. Several were wearing high school sweaters, and I found that I knew half a dozen of them. I asked them where they were going, and they said they were going to the coast, or to new Ontario. When they got up to the mines in Ontario and the west they found the work being done by foreigners, and they could not get jobs. As a result

The Budget-Mr. Church
they were locked up, all because of the policy followed by this parliament of divesting itself of responsibility. We might just as well go home and let the house of Purvis and the du Pont dynasty run the affairs of the country. We might as well close up here if we are going to allow Mr. Purvis to lord it over the municipal representatives and members of parliament from the province of Ontario. I know something about the mishandling of this employment question, and when I see these men being driven out of their homes while this parliament does nothing for them I think the time has come to say something in this house, whether the Minister of Labour likes it or not.
Last year I made some constructive suggestions to the minister in this regard. I told him he should do as was done by the government in 1919; he should add a clause in the act by which these agreements could be made directly with the municipalities. The previous minister, a very able man, Hon. Mr. Gordon, who was Minister of Labour and Mines, did ten times the work that is being done by the present minister; he tided us over the worst five years of the depression. You could telephone to him and any municipal officer could get relief at once, but the situation is different to-day. You have to run around after this Purvis commission, this travelling minstrel show which is touring the country. At one time I was in a minstrel show myself; I know something about how such shows are run, and I can tell you that the amateur minstrel show at the old Grand opera house with which I was connected could not be compared with Mr. Purvis and his minstrels, who are travelling from Vancouver to Halifax. In the United States one man can handle all that work, and something has been done over there. It is true that they have made mistakes, but conditions are not the same.
Let me tell my hon. friend that I sat in this house from 1921 to 1930, when the Liberal party was in power. What did they do? Every session a speech from the throne was delivered, but the subject of unemployment was never mentioned during the nine years they were in office. On December 14, 1926, I said:
I very much regret that in the speech from the throne the government have given no indication that they are going to take any active steps to solve the economic ills of this country. There is the problem, for instance, of unemployment. Unemployment to-day in the larger centres of population is very acute. I might refer to the unemployment in the large manufacturing city from which I come. I know the conditions there, and I know that in the
past few days very rapid preparations have been made by the social and charitable institutions and public bodies of various kinds in the city to try and cope with the unemployment situation with which we shall be faced this coming winter. I regret, I say, that the government in the speech from the throne has announced no definite policy for taking care of the economic ills in the larger centres of population in this country.
I asked the then minister of labour, Mr. Heenan, who is now in another house, whether the government had made any plans for providing work for the unemployed, .and whether or not the government were prepared to contribute one-third of the cost of relief. Mr. Heenan in reply to me said the government would do nothing, that it would be contrary to the British North America Act, and that this was a matter for the provinces. Then I asked if the government would appoint a royal commission, as was done in 1927, in the United States senate, about a month later on the motion of the late mayor of Detroit, Senator Couzens. When the depression came on they were ready, but the government here said there was no unemployment, and that if there was it was a matter for the provinces. So nothing was done right down\ to 1930. The government refused to have count of the unemployed taken, with the result that when the late government came into* office they had nothing before them. During: the five years hon. gentlemen opposite wera in opposition they did not treat* the government as the present government is being treated by the right hon. leader of the opposition. Oh, no; they threw cold water on the social legislation and unemployment insurance and put all kinds of stumbling blocks in the way, with the result that we have the present condition of affairs.
The judgments that have been rendered by the privy council after all are only opinions having to do with abstract and not with concrete questions and are only dicta and opinions. Sickness and unemployment insurance was part of the Liberal platform of 1919, but this Liberal government was in power from 1921 to 1930 without making an attempt to bring in that insurance. That scheme has been in operation in England since 1910, and as a result England was better prepared for the depression than any [DOT] other country. The supreme court divided three to two on the question of unemployment insurance; the two strongest judges said we could grant money under the first part of section 91, having to do with "public debt and property." What is the use of the Minister of Labour talking about the provinces
The Budget-Mr. Church
