speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he has spoken for forty minutes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I would like to read a telegram which I received this morning from Leduc, Alberta. It reads:
Due to the fact that the importation of vegetable oils to be used as shortening in the place of butter and lard is seriously damaging the markets for these products in Canada we respectfully urge you to support the national Dairy Council in its application for a special duty on such oils.
Gus Lingert,
W. L. Perley,
H. Hamilton,
R. Hetsler,
John I. Wanicka,
Algot Pearson,
O. Bostrom,
E. O. Weedman,
E. W. Roth,
Arthur Pearson,
E. S. Anderson,
E. A. Westlund.
It is said that unemployment is the greatest problem we have to face in Canada. I believe that to be true. It has been said in this house that the only way to preserve our democracy is to put everyone to work. I do not believe that is so; in fact I believe the very reverse to be true. What are the facts? Everybody has been put to work in Russia, in Germany and in Italy, and in every one of th%se countries democracy has ceased to exist. Everybody has not been put to work in the British Empire or in the United States, and in these countries democracy still exists. I think we must accept the idea of permanent unemployment and must make provision for it.
I do not wish to take up any time in discussing ways and means of curing or providing for unemployment, but I should like to suggest one very simple and obvious thing to do, and that is to lower the age at which old age pensions are paid. What is the sense of making men of seventy work when there are hundreds of thousands of young men idle? I do not know to what age this limit should be reduced, but to start with I would suggest sixty years. I know I shall be told that this is not a wise thing to do, and I shall be asked, where is the money to come from? That is the invariable question. If I may make a further suggestion it would be this. I would say to
The Budget-Mr. Jaques

those who control the finances of the country: "Gentlemen, we have received a mandate from the people of Canada to end poverty and unemployment. We believe that it is mainly a question of finance. You claim a monopoly of the knowledge of money, and certainly you enjoy a monopoly of creating it. We are going to give you the job of financing the provision for unemployment which, by your very policies, you have mainly brought about. We will give you reasonable time to do this, and meantime we will sharpen your wits. We propose to license financial institutions, all branches and branch managers, accepting at first a nominal licence fee. But if at the end of, say, a year you have not arrived at a solution we shall multiply that fee one thousand times, and will use the money to take care of the unemployed." The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) told us of the increased business prosperity of Canada, which I believe to be more apparent than real, and claimed the credit was due to the tariff policies of the government. I do not agree with him. I believe any improvement in business there may be is due to a policy of easy money, behind a smoke screen of trade agreements. Since I have been in Canada I have heard questions of tariff and free trade debated, and all I want to say is that if you quote the opinions of fifty of the most eminent business men who are in favour of free trade I will quote the words of fifty equally eminent men who are in favour of protection. I have the advantage over some members of having lived part of my life in a totally free trade country, and another part in protected Canada. When I lived in England, which of course was then under free trade, I enjoyed financial independence; and certainly for people in that position free trade is a fine thing. One's money goes a long way. But there is another side to the picture: there is the horrible and disgusting poverty behind the scenes; and whatever hon. members opposite may say about free trade, this much is certain, that during a policy of free trade the slums of England, Scotland and Wales were developed. I do not say the free trade policy was the only cause of slums, but certainly it did not prevent them. When as a young man I came to Canada I soon learned that my money did not go so far as it did in England. I found that a shilling was equal to about seventy-five cents. In spite of that fact, I do not think anyone will question that at the beginning of the century the masses of the people were better off in protected Canada than they were in free trade England. I believe there is no 
doubt about that, and the fact that Canada attracted hundreds of thousands of British people is proof of it.
However, I would hesitate to say the same thing to-day. I believe that particularly at the present time as a place in which to live, England is more attractive than Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But they have not free trade now.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is true. The fact that England has adopted a policy of protection may or may not be the cause of it.
May I say a few words about inflation? Whenever any monetary reform is suggested, at once we are told about inflation. That is the bogey to frighten the naughty children. But we never hear anything about the evils of deflation. I believe the obvious reason is that those who enjoy financial independence, those who have good salaries and who control finance, do very well during times of deflation. Their money goes farther, and prices are lower, but at the expense of those who produce the wealth of Canada. I represent thousands of people who in the last seven years, through a policy of deflation, have been utterly ruined. The work of a lifetime has been swept away, and from a position of economic independence, hundreds of thousands of people in western Canada have been brought to ruin simply because deflation has made it impossible except at a loss to produce the wealth of the country. What we need is a system which will avoid the evils of inflation and1 those of deflation, but certainly that is not possible under a system of orthodox finance.
Then we have the good old velocity of circulation. Of course, that is a smoke screen to hide a shortage of money. When we say there is a shortage of money we are told that there is enough of it, but that it does not circulate quickly enough. May I be permitted to read the definition of velocity of circulation as stated by Professor D. B. Copland, doctor of science, and an eminent economist:
A given unit of money will circulate many times in a unit of time. It will make many payments because it has what economists call velocity of circulation.
May I illustrate the point with a story? It seems that two Irishmen, Pat and Mike, invested' in a keg of beer which they were going to retail at the local race meet. As they had only ten cents left after buying the beer they found they had to carry it to the track. It was a hot day with a bright sun overhead. Pat, who had the ten cents, said to Mike, "Sell me a drink of beer," and paid

The Budget-Mr. Jaques
over to Mike the ten cents for the drink. Of course that made Mike thirsty, and he said to Pat, "Sell me a glass of beer," and passed the ten cents back to Pat. And since it was a hot day, it was not long before the ten cents had passed a good many times and the keg was empty. I think hon. members will agree with me that, given two Irishmen and a keg of beer and a hot day, you would have a very satisfactory and satisfying velocity of circulation. That is a perfectly good illustration of the velocity of circulation theory, but what I should like to be told is this: How does ten cents recoup Pat and Mike for their beer, and how does it replace the beer? It will replace ten. cents' worth of beer and no more.
We are also given the illustration of the baker who takes in, say fifty dollars; he runs across to the butcher and spends the fifty dollars. The butcher, we are told, goes to the hardware merchant and spends the fifty dollars there; the hardware merchant goes to the grocer, and so on, so that according to this argument the same fifty dollars will do hundreds of dollars' worth of business. But it will do nothing of the sort. One dollar will liquidate one dollar's worth of debt and no more. And it is easy to see the reason. The money issues from, a bank as a debt through production, and it is paid out in wages and salaries to the public. There is no other source of purchasing power than wages, salaries and dividends. The public take their wages and salaries and dividends to the local storekeeper or to the theatre and buy what they need with it. As soon as it crosses the counter it is on its way back to where it started from, and a cancellation results. So, as Major Douglas says, it is a complete fallacy to suppose that one dollar of purchasing power can liquidate nore than one dollar's worth of debts.
There is another subject about which I have heard a great deal in this house, and that is the subject of thrift, hard work, " tightening your belt " and working harder. But it seems to me that we have forgotten the meaning of the word " thrift." Thrift, I think, means to thrive. If we travel about Canada we see little evidence of any real thrift. I have travelled a great deal this last year, and, looking out of the windows, what have I seen? Thousands of miles of forest destroyed by the axe or by fire, hundreds of thousands of acres of wind-blown and weed-infested land, thousands of buildings rotting from lack of paint, idle plants, idle machinery, and idle men. Yet we pride ourselves on being a thrifty people! As a matter of fact
we are not thrifty; we are thriftless. Thrift in the modern sense means saving money. I suggest that that is not thrift; it is avarice, and I believe that avarice, or the hoarding of money, has caused more human misery than all the forces of nature combined. A man saves money, that is he refrains from consuming, and to that extent goods cannot be sold. We are told, of course, that to-day money which is saved is invested, so that if one person does not spend it somebody else will. That is not quite true. When money is invested it is paid out in wages and salaries in respect of a fresh cycle of production, and on its way to the consumer's pockets again it lays a fresh trail of costs. The same lot of money cannot liquidate two lots of costs; in other words, you have two lots of goods and only one lot of money.
Of course saving is the only individual remedy for financial insecurity, but at the same time it is, I believe, a social evil of the worst kind. It is all right for the individual to save for a rainy day, but when the individual saves for a rainy day and numbers of individuals do likewise they are bringing about a continuous wet spell for increasing numbers of people.	The same reasoning
applies to insurance of all kinds. I am perfectly well aware that the only security which the individual can command is his insurance. At the same time he does so to a very large extent at the expense of the community. And so with unemployment insurance: that, it seems to me, if it were adopted would lead to an increase of unemployment; it would represent poverty, and surely we do not want to represent poverty, we want to abolish it.
And what is the workman to save? I am not speaking of men who are lucky enough to have so much money that they simply cannot spend it; of course they must save and invest it. Neither do I advocate taking that excess money from those people. There is no need of that; we are glad that there are at least some people who have enough. But consider the average wage earner, receiving about seventy dollars per month, who is told that he should put aside part of his wages to insure himself against unemployment or against old age. What I want to know is, what is he going to save? From a national standpoint there is no need to save money, considering money to-day-in spite of the denials-as simply figures in a book.	As
there is no need to save that, is he to save his food and his clothes? When he is in the heyday of his strength is he to save for his old age, his overalls, some clothes and some
The Budget-Mr. Jaques

food which will either be mouldy or rotten when he needs them? Where is the point in saving? How can he save without bringing about a shortage of purchasing power?
Consider a community on an island. We will say that they have been shipwrecked. For a considerable time those people will be put to it to supply themselves with the necessities of life. It will take the efforts of all to keep themselves alive. But if they have any intelligence, sooner or later somebody will say, for instance, "If we had a boat and a net one of us could catch all the fish that we need and the rest of us could devote ourselves to something else." That would be a case of real saving. In order to build the boat and make the net, the community would have to put aside some other work until the boat was built; but when the boat was finished, of course, they would have the advantage of it and more time to devote to other things. But meantime they must save on their production in order to build the boat. That was true so long as the world was in an age of real scarcity. But suppose we want to build a boat to-day: where is the point in saving money for it? If we do we are going to cause a certain amount of unemployment in the meantime, because goods to that extent cannot be sold. And what do we need to save labour for when there is labour and machinery to spare? There is no need to lay anyone off to build the boat because there are hundreds of thousands, not to say millions, of men looking for the job. We could build hundreds of boats, we could make practically everything we need without saving a cent. I suggest that the mere fact of saving is one of the causes of unemployment and poverty. I do not mean to suggest that we should prohibit or attempt to prohibit saving and insurance, but I do suggest that care must be taken to see that those who must save and want to save can do so without penalizing the rest of the community.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke some days ago he quoted certain well-known lines of Shakespeare. I will read only three:
Neither a borrower nor a lender be;
For loan oft loses both itself and friend,
And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
And the right hon. gentleman spoke these words of his own:
I say to those who hesitate to realize the stature to which Canada has thus far advanced, and what is expected of her as a nation, they will do well to heed and to apply to our country the words of profound wisdom addressed by Polonius to his son Laertes, as Laertes set out upon his own.

Having been the victim of borrowing for purposes of production, I know full well the truth that borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry. People are encouraged to borrow money when money is plentiful; in fact, that is the only time they can borrow; and if they are enterprising they want of course to branch out and enlarge their operations. Things look good, times are promising, money is easy and they borrow. But when they come to pay back they find that money has become tight, scarce, and their prices have fallen, so that they cannot pay and their security is lost. That has been the story of the farming people whom I represent here.
The blame for the poverty in the west is put entirely on one thing, the drought. That is not true of my riding. The riding which I represent has never suffered from drought; the farmers have had fairly good crops right along. But they have had to market their crops at about twenty-five per cent of what it cost to produce them. I myself have delivered perfectly good barley at seven cents a bushel, and it cost me six cents to thresh it. That is why the farmers of northern Alberta and northern Saskatchewan are in the condition they are in to-day. The policy of deflation, sound money, has made it impossible for them to pay their debts; and then, to add insult to injury, they are called dishones't. If we are to bring about and maintain any kind of permanent prosperity, one of the most obvious things to do is this. When people borrow money the money must be available with which to pay back. And I would add, in closing, words of even more profound wisdom tfian Shakespeare's-the love of money is the root of all evil.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, I wish at the outset to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on his budget. I shall not attempt to discuss it in detail. I shall leave that task to hon. members who are better informed and more experienced than I am.
I wish also to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and all the members of his government on the unceasing and strenuous efforts they have made to improve the situation of the country. Their efforts have not been in vain, for, ever since the Liberal party came into power, a new confidence has arisen among the people of Canada and conditions have improved to a remarkable extent. Our trade has increased, our industrial production has expanded as a result of the opening of new markets, and our railway traffic has felt the initial effects

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe (Matapedia)
of the policies now in force. But in spite of these general improvements it must be admitted that we are still far from the prosperity at which we all aim. Indeed our agricultural and labouring classes, for whom the depression has been most severe, are still suffering keenly.
The wages paid to certain classes of workers, especially in the rural districts, are entirely out of proportion to the cost of living. For instance I cannot conceive of a family with eight children living on an income of $1.50 a day. It is hardly enough to provide decent food; what then is left for clothing, shelter, taxes, and other necessities? Real prosperity cannot be expected so long as the purchasing power of the masses is not increased, and it cannot increase so long as our working classes are not paid better wages. I do not pretend to be an economist, but I believe I have acquired during my lifetime a certain experience that has been denied to some. I have known the poverty of the masses through having shared it myself, and if I feel so deeply for our humble workers who put in many hours of arduous toil for a wage of SI.50 it is because of the understanding I have of their lamentable situation. How often have I been profoundly moved at the sad stories of poor workingmen who complained to me of their sufferings and hardships, and whose complaints I found to be fully justified. Our labouring classes have long been demanding reasonable wages, wages which would allow them to improve their situation and to look to the future with greater hope, but they are tired of waiting for reforms that are essential but are so long in coming. In an age when colossal fortunes are being built up so rapidly, it is only right that our poor workingmen should be paid wages sufficient to provide their families with at least a minimum of the comforts of life.
One of the most pressing duties of any government anxious to maintain our internal peace is to take drastic measures to end such shocking abuses as those which have been revealed in the past few years. In passing I wish to congratulate once more the Prime Minister upon having ordered the investigation, which has been conducted with such firmness, of the textile industry. The present century has been called a century of progress, but to me it seems a century of slavery and crying social injustice such as the world has perhaps never seen before. At the rate we are now going, if governments do not bring about extensive reforms to end the present abuses the most frightful disaster will inevitably overtake us.
I wish to take the opportunity of my participation in this debate to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to the lamentable situation in which a large number of farmers and agricultural workers in my constituency find themselves as a result of the bad weather conditions of last summer, followed by early frosts which prevented their crops from ripening. In some parishes at least seventy-five per cent of our farmers will not have any seed this spring, and unless something is done to assist them a large number will be ruined.
I shall now conclude my remarks in the French language, and I trust that the right hon. leader of the opposition will not consider that as a concession.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I now wish to revert to a subject which I mentioned during the last session and which is most important for the future welfare of eastern Quebec. I am referring to the development of natural t resources in the hinterland of Gaspe peninsula, which offer great posibilities. I am absolutely convinced that if we were to study thoroughly this plan and give it due consideration, we would find in it a solution to our unemployment problem in a good many counties.
Gaspe peninsula, known to thousands of Canadian and American tourists who visit it each year is a really delightful country, covers all that part of the province of Quebec which is bounded on the north and northeast by the St. Lawrence gulf, on the south by Chaleur bay, and on the west by the Matapedia valley.	It includes the large
constituencies of Gaspe, Bonaventure, and Matapedia-Matane.	From Pointe a Pere
to the mouth of the Metis river it is 190 miles long; its width is about 85 miles, and its area, more than 12,000 miles.
In so far as its climate is concerned, one must not base his opinion on the remarks I made a few moments ago, for the weather last year, was quite exceptional. Gaspe's climate cold as it may be reputed to be, has a favouring influence on plant life. In winter it is dry and healthy, and in summer, sufficiently favourable to ensure the ripening of the crops. Excessive heat is unknown in that district. Gaspe's climate might be compared to that of Sault Ste Marie, in Ontario, or that of Edmonton, in Alberta.
The south shore of the peninsula is served by three railway sections which are now part of the Canadian National Railways and which are as follows: from Mont Joli to Matapedia, the old Intercolonial; from Matapedia to New-Carlisle, the Quebec Western; and from New Carlisle to Gaspe, the Quebec Oriental and Atlantic.
1482	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Lapointe (Matapedia)
The north shore has no railways, except its western end which is served for a distance of 36 miles, namely from Mont Joli to Matane, by the Canada & Gulf Terminal Railway. As to the hinterland, there are no transportation facilities. It remained in a wild state just as it was when Jacques Cartier discovered Canada, 400 years ago. However, it is not for lack of natural wealth, and it is this natural wealth which I would now like to dwell upon.
The lofty Shickshoeks range, with peaks reaching up to 4,000 feet, runs across the peninsula on the greatest part of its length. On this high Shickshoeks range, at about two thirds of its width from Chaleur bay, there are two plateaus spreading one towards the north, the other towards the south. The headwaters which are draining that part of the country bear the following names: Nou-velle, Cascapedia, Bonaventure, Pabos, St. John and York.
It is estimated that 85 to 90 per cent of the district is wooded country. These forests of the Gaspe peninsula might contain approximately 40 million cords of soft wood, balsam and spruce, or 20 billion feet b.m. of lumber, and about one billion feet of hard wood and pine. These forests constitute the greatest timber wealth of eastern Quebec, but they have now attained their full growth, and moreover they are now subject to attacks from pests and other foes of the tree. Therefore, if they are not developed in the very near future, it will be an incalculable loss for our province and the country at large.
Forest fires also caused considerable damage in the Gaspe peninsula. It is worth noting that most of .the big fires which broke out did most damage in the centre part of the peninsula where development after a fire was practically impossible, which meant a total loss. Since 1916, it is estimated that about 5,000.000 cords of pulwood were thus destroyed. If you only value a cord at $5, you will realize what enormous amount that represents. If you add the loss brought about by pests which are causing considerable damage, as well as the rapidly increasing depreciation of the trees after they are fully grown, you will realize what immense wealth we are thus wasting through our inaction. I maintain that our governments have no right to forsake and waste such plentiful resources which Providence has placed at our disposal, particularly at a time when thousands of unemployed are daman-ding work.
Having considered Gaspe's timber resources I shall now turn to its mineral possibilities. Around 1854, Sir William Logan was sent

there in quest of coal. It was in the course of that survey that oil was spotted out, first around Gaspe, from the York river district down near cape St. Pierre. According to more recent surveys, the oil fields would seem to spread from Gaspe bay to the Matapedia valley. As regards mineral ores, they have been found in large quantities all over the peninsula. Gold and silver bearing ores were found along the York river, at Marsouins, Cross Point, but they did not carry their search any further. During the last few years, the investigations have rather had to do with lead and zinc along Berry brook, a tributary to the Cascapedia. Numerous veins with a satisfactory content were found since 1909. They found in Deslandes and Lesseps townships chrome iron pyrites bearing some splendid iron. Although the investigations were not carried on very far, asbestos was found at St. Moise, at Matapedia, and also in the townships of Blanchet, Courcelette and Weir. Almost everywhere there is plenty of granite for building purposes. Some blocks have been known to measure 8 feet in diameter and to reach up to 350 feet in length. Moreover, there is marble, limestone and sandstone of the best quality. Notwithstanding the investigations that were carried on more for examination than development purposes, geologists are in agreement as to the zinc, lead and copper resources of the Gaspe peninsula. One of them, Alcock, noted some copper bearing fields in Tessier and St. Denis townships, in Matane county and in the York river district. Others suggested in their reports to undertake more extensive surveys and prospection on a large scale in those districts.
It will thus be seen that Gaspe's resources are real. But we lack the necessary means for their development. At the present time, prospection and development cannot be actively carried on. owing to the many difficulties to be overcome in reaching the centre of the peninsula. There are no transportation facilities and prospectors must carry on their backs their equipment and food over narrow trails that are blocked up most of the time. If communications were easier, it would be possible to undertake more exhaustive investigations, to work the mines already discovered and to find new ones. The results that have been achieved so far, were obtained with the greatest difficulty. The gold mines of Ontario and northern Quebec offered no greater opportunities than those of the Gaspe district, but transportation facilities made their development possible.
So, Gaspe peninsula where, so far, only incomplete investigations have been made, where only a bird's eye view, as it were, has been

The Budget-Mr. Lapointe (Matapedia)
taken, shows every indication of a mineral wealth which only awaits human intervention to reveal itself and become a valuable economic asset for Canada as a whole. Gaspe peninsula could become the most important mining centre of eastern Quebec, which would increase our national welfare.
Besides the wealth which I have just mentioned, the Gaspe district has great possibilities from the standpoint of agriculture and colonization. According to the geologist Alcock, the Gaspe district has a most fertile soil. It would appear that the peninsula has enough land for 40 or 60 new parishes. It would be the most suitable place for carrying into effect a comprehensive colonization scheme, which would relieve our population in our older parishes and afford room for our farmers' sons, who would find there the necessary land and the proper conditions for the development of their energy and ability.
The Gaspe district has many other resources, but let me mention only its long famed fisheries, its splendid rivers, its wonderful seaports through which the goods produced inland could be shipped. It is one of those few regions wdiich lack almost nothing and are practically self-sufficient.
Since we still have acute unemployment, since all those remedies which have been used so far have proved to be mere palliatives, and have not given the expected results, since this unemployment calamity threatens more and more to disorganize our economic system, why not consider a scheme for the development of our resources on a large scale? How many countries would like to own the wonderful heritage with which Providence has blessed us, in order to make it productive.
Industry will never be able to absorb all our working men. Yet, it is imperative that we should give up that baneful policy of relief, initiated by' the former government, which has spoiled our people in teaching them to rely upon the nation for their upkeep.
Therefore. Mr. Speaker, work is what we need. Work for our honest unemployed who are courageous and find it humiliating to appeal unceasingly for help. Work for our young people who are losing their spirit through idleness. At a time when there is so much unrest, when so many false prophets are propagating their nefarious doctrines throughout the world, we must necessarily draw our young people from the harmful environment in which they now live. Otherwise, we would be turning this rising generation into a communistic and revolutionary class. To all those who are courageous and proud, to all those
who are industrious and wish to get on in the world, we should hold out new prospects. To all these people, the great Gaspe district opens a wide field of activity, provided the governments will make it accessible for them.
And here is what I suggest: a five-year plan through which the federal and provincial governments would each spend, in cooperation, $500,000 a year, first to provide transportation facilities consisting at first in a highway along the centre of the whole peninsula, its starting points being, from the St. Lawrence river, Matane, and from the Matapedia valley either Sayabec, Val-Brillant, Amqui or Lac au Saumon. Then, mineral prospection on a large scale, the opening up of regions suitable for settlement and the development of accessible forests, and after that, the building of a railroad which would then be, I am quite sure, considered as absolutely necessary.
Air. Speaker, in the past, the province of Quebec has not been pampered like some other provinces as regards railways. To-day, she would need hundreds of millions to make up for the lost time. And in order to see whether our claim is justified, it is only necessary to look over our railway maps and to compare them to those of other provinces. Eastern Quebec was never treated fairly in that respect, and Gaspe has been especially overlooked. That district has been lamentably disregarded by all the successive governments in this country.
That is the reason why, in spite of the countless wealth which is to be found in Gaspe, that region, which is as vast as some kingdoms, has not developed at the same rate as the rest of the country. At various times, its people have been compelled to go into exile, because they could not make a living or find enough room on that land which, however, they loved so much.
Will our governments decide at last to hear the claims of Gaspe. that land full of promise which for so many years has been overlooked and forgotten? I am confident that the present government which, I know, is quite favourably disposed, will give its best attention to the suggestions I have just made and find it possible to carry out the plan which I have just outlined in this house. Then our old land of Gaspe will awake from her slumber of the past four centuries. And for our younger generation, dispirited by those six years of depression, this will mean the dawn of a new and better day. and for our thousands of unemployed, who live in poverty, it will bring the prospect of more prosperous times to which they have been looking forward for so long.
The Budget-Mr. Perley

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be impossible for me to review in detail in forty minutes the many important questions raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in his budget speech. Therefore, I shall endeavour to confine myself to those problems which pertain particularly to western Canada. The minister expressed hopes for a bright fiscal year in 1937-38. If things are to improve as he thinks they are, why did he not endeavour to give some encouragement to the consumers of Canada by reducing some of the forms of taxation? I refer particularly to the sales tax which, as the minister stated, represents about thirty per cent of the total income of the government. A one per cent reduction would have meant $15,000,000 which the consumer would not have to pay, and a two per cent reduction would have meant something worth while to the consumer.
The minister stated that the financial picture was much better and he was particularly pleased to announce that the wheat board had repaid all government and bank advances and other obligations and were returning 18,000,000 to the dominion treasury. I am sure it will be interesting for the farmers of western Canada to note that, as $3,000,000 of it will be used to return the five per cent cut to the civil servants.
I should like to draw the attention of this house to the importance of the agricultural industry. Unless the farmers of Canada, and the farmers of western Canada in particular, are prosperous, Canada cannot bp prosperous. The three prairie provinces have produced as much as one billion dollars worth of new wealth in a year. The average annual production of new wealth during the past ten years has been $700,000,000. Hon. members can readily appreciate what that means to industry in eastern Canada and to the railways through the carriage of freight.
In the few remarks I have to make I intend to deal more particularly with wheat. Our difficulties of marketing this and other grains began in 1929-30. Because of the depression, the wheat importing countries of the world took less wheat and we in Canada found ourselves in difficulties. Some of the leading wheat companies, particularly the pool, found themselves in difficulty in 1930. I shall not review all that the previous government did in dealing with this problem, nor do I think it is necessary for me to cover all that occurred prior to the passing of the wheat board act in 1935 because I think all this is well within thp memoiy of nearly every hon. member. Suffice it to say that Mr. McFarland was
TMr A. J. Lapointe.]
in charge from 1930 to 1935 when the wheat board act came into force. During that period he not only handled the surplus which he took over in 1930, but he added considerably to that surplus because of the stabilization operations which he conducted. The government was asked to allow him to conduct these operations by boards of trade, municipal organizations, banks, wheat pools, the grain exchange and other organizations in western Canada. I shall state only this fact, that Mr. Mclvor appearing before the committee investigating the Canadian Wheat Board Act, passed in 1935, gave evidence, in answer to a question I put to him, to the effect that the McFarland operations had meant at least 15 cents a bushel on all the wheat which had been grown in a four-year period in western Canada, over and above what the farmer would have received if he had not carried on those operations.
In the month of October, 1935, there was a change of government, and a change in the wheat board. .Mr. Murray was put in charge, as chairman. I make this statement: From the first day he took over he pursued a fire sale policy with respect to the surplus and the selling of wheat. We knew Mr. Murray quite well; we know that he was the man who had informed Mr. Ralston, when Mr. Ralston made the charges. It was he who supplied Mr. Ralston with the information he used, and in making the charges Mr. Ralston often used the expresion "if I am correctly informed" or "if information given me is correct," and we knew from where that intormation came.
I shall deal with three things that Mr. Murray did when he first took over, and as matters went along, to show conclusively that he pursued a fire sale policy. He took office on December 5, and the first sale is recorded on December 9. One of the first things he did in taking office was to make an agreement with the members of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, or a committee of it. The agreement is to be found at page 259 of the evidence taken last year. I would ask hon. members to pay attention to the second paragraph of the agreement, which reads as follows:-
No. 2. The board are willing to agree to the second suggestion made by the exporters committee: namely, that the board will make wheat available to exporters in sufficient quantity to cover their overnight acceptances during the first ten minutes after the opening of the market, at not more than i cent over the previous day's close.
The wording suggests that they accepted the suggestion made by the committee of the

The Budget-Mr. Perley
grain exchange, and the basis of the agreement was production of offers and acceptances.
I wish further to draw this to the attention of the house. At page 508 of Hansard for this session hon. members will see that the agreement was made without the knowledge of the government, and that the agreement which was cancelled ten days later was cancelled without the knowledge of the government. That was the reply to the question I had asked.
Following the agreement being made, sales were made on the 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th and so on. On December 13 he sold 22,025,000 bushels of wheat, 8,500,000 or more of which was delivered under the terms of the agreement. That was the morning that word was received in Winnipeg that the Argentine market had increased 19 cents, and Liverpool was up 7. It is interesting to note that that agreement was cancelled, however, on the 20th, and the sales following the cancellation of the agreement dropped from millions to thousands. On December 23, there were 333,000 bushels of wheat sold; on December 24, 371,000; and on February 28 it dropped to 51,000. I claim that that is evidence that he was playing into the hands of the members of the exchange.
Owing to that sale on December 13, the leader of the opposition made a charge on the floor of the House of Commons after the house met last year. On February 13 I made a statement that when the committee was investigating we would demand the production of these offers and acceptances as proof of sale. I may say we never received them before the committee. If hon. members will look at page 307 of the evidence they will find that in reply to my question the chairman stated that those documents had never been in the hands of the government or the wheat board, and that Mr. Murray also stated he was unable to produce them. In their place they produced an auditors' report, which is a most interesting document. It was tabled before the committee, is dated March 6, and states the cause of the delay was that they had to communicate with the principals of certain companies in the old country in order to get the offers and acceptances, and documents necessary to offer as proof of sale. That is two and a half months after.
There is a second matter I should like to draw to the attention of the house, and it is this: On December 12, a day or two after he took over, he dispatched Mr. Cecil Lamont to the old country. Mr. Lamont had a letter of some importance to British millers and
importers, to one or two parts of which I shall refer. The letter is to be found at page 145 of the evidence. As it is long I shall not attempt to read it all, but one paragraph states he may inform the British millers that the fixed minimum price paid producers by the board does not necessarily bear any relation to the board's selling price. Another paragraph states that he may inform the British millers what the board considers a fair value or premium for Canadian wheat as compared with other wheats, and that the board does not agree that the premium at which our wheat had been held in the past two years was a fair premium. I say that shows clearly they were anxious to sell our wheat at almost any price.
That letter, which I call the Lamont letter, cost the farmers of western Canada at least 820,000.000. Here is my reason for making the statement: I have myself, personally- not second hand-been in conversation with representatives of British millers. In conversation with a representative of a subsidiary company of Joseph Ranke and Company within the last three months I asked about the Lamont letter. The person to whom I spoke knew it almost word for word. I asked him what he considered it meant. He said they interpreted it as an invitation to bid for the wheat at anything less than the fixed minimum price. I asked him how much he considered it had lowered the purchase price, and he replied that it was at least ten cents, and possibly nearer fifteen cents. He indicated to me that they had purchased the wheat at from ten to fifteen cents a bushel less, from the date they saw that letter until July 31 last year. That is a serious matter, and I give the circumstances from first-hand information.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Second-hand.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is secondhand to you, but it came first-hand to me. May I say here and now that if hon. members review the evidence they will find that last year there was produced before the committee a statement from a certain Rotterdam firm as to the low price at which the Canadian government was selling its wheat. The Australian government had protested. There were many evidences that the board was underselling the market.
A committee was set up last year, and may I point out an interesting fact in connection with its work. When the committee met and organized on March 24 they sent for Mr. Murray, but Mr. Murray wrote a letter, dated March 26, to the secretary of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, a copy of which I have in my hand. In that letter he states:
The Budget-Mr. Perley

The Canadian wheat board will continue, as far as they are able to do so, cooperating with the trade in spreading as well as other marketing operations. . . . The next spread will be Jifly-October, and we wish to suggest to the trade that they should consider if it is desirable for them to continue depending blindly on the board for all or any particular part of this spread.
That was a nice invitation to the members of the grain exchange, just before he departed for Ottawa to appear before the committee. In my opinion it was an absolutely improper statement on his part. In effect he was saying to the trade, "You need not worry; we are going to take care of you. It does not matter about the investigation or anything else."
The report of the committee which investigated this subject last year is an interesting document. It recites, first, that a full examination of Mr. Murray was conducted, and that in selling wheat he was complying with the policy the government had in view when it set up the wheat board. The second paragraph is as follows:
While there was a short interest in the Winnipeg wheat market in December of 1935. no evidence was produced that would warrant the conclusion that speculative short interests were protected by the board in that month. As the committee finds it impracticable to obtain conclusive evidence on this point, we recommend that this matter be referred for further investigation to the Royal Commission, the appointment of which is recommended in this report.
There is the reason for the Turgeon commission, the commission which has been inquiring for several months into the grain trade, yet I have not seen in the published reports of the evidence they have been taking any reference to this important matter, the first thing they were asked to consider. It is not necessary for me to say anything about the cost of the inquiry. Mr. Ralston, who from his seat on the opposition benches repeatedly rose to oppose the passing of this act,-than whom no man was more bitter in opposition to it-is to-day employed at the handsome figure of $200 per day and $20 expenses to make these inquiries. It will cost this country more to pay his salary for one month than the farmers of Saskatchewan will pay in income tax in a year.
Mr. Murray's report of his operations to January 1 of this year is very interesting, not for what it contains but for what it omits. He first refers to the dismissal of the old board and of the advisory committee, but he does not in that report tell the public that upon the dismissal of the advisory committee its place was taken by a committee of four members of this cabinet. On the third page

he asserts that there will be no fire sale policy pursued by the board. The fact that they sold in one day 22,000,000 bushels of wheat, and the further fact that in about ten days they sold over 40,000,000 bushels of wheat, gives some evidence of fire sale methods. In two months, December, 1935 and July, 1936, they sold 113,000,000 bushels. I wish to draw attention to the fact that in July of last year the board sold in the neighbourhood of 63,000,000 bushels of wheat, when there was every evidence that there would be a very substantial increase in price and practically a crop failure all over the western states and the southern part of the prairie provinces. I hold in my hand a copy of a daily report issued by the crop reporters who go through the west during the growing season and, report on the crop situation. Here are some extracts:
July 1-Hot, dry weather over western Canada will make a general and serious reduction in the crop in the prairie provinces.
July 3-For the third time in the last six years, drought is destroying the spring wheat crops in thp United States.
July 4-The increased alarm in the United States over the drought situation has a deep interest in western Canada.
July 6-A week-end of unrelenting dry heat in western Canada and the spring grain areas of the United States saw wheat prices on the Winnipeg grain exchange pushed forward to the five cent limit.
July 8-Tom Moody, North Dakota, W.P.A. administrator, stood to-day in the tower of the state capital at Bismark and said that the drought was worse than the one in 1934, and was causing more damage than anything in the memory of the oldest pioneer.
It goes on through the whole month.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member read to the house the report that Mr. McFarland gave out in the middle of June, when he said the crop would amount to over 400,000.000 bushels?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When I went home from this parliament last year a splendid crop was growing on my own farm, but it did not amount to anything. When the hot weather struck it in the early part of July, it practically petered out. We know that there was a splendid prospect in June.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Could the hon. member give us Mr. McFarland's prophecy along with the others?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and there were a lot of others who made prophecies of a good crop. In 1935 we had a splendid crop of grain almost until the binder was ready to go into the field, and then rust took it. From that it will be seen how soon a crop in western Canada can peter out.

The Budget-Mr. Perley
July 9-Western Canadian farmers should rise up and arrange an injunction against the Canadian wheat board and prevent the board selling any more wheat under $1.25 a bushel, as a result of present crop prospects.
Each day there is a similar report.
July 18-All the information that is obtain-[DOT] able at this trading centre suggests that the government board will sell its last bushel of carry-over at the market. . . . But, in the very midst of the scorching heat wave, with every surface indication of a reduced crop in Canada and utter destruction over a wide area in the central States, the Winnipeg market declined four cents! Why? Government wheat board selling.
Later, this report states that during the month the wheat board had thrown into the Winnipeg pit 60,000,000 bushels of wheat.
But even the market itself, under that flood of wheat, did its level best to show that throwing that immense bushelage into speculators' hands between July 1 and July 31, 1936, was not a sales policy at all, but was a crime against the producers.
Four of the large firms in the Winnipeg exchange participated, no doubt more than they should have, in the profits that were made through the government board selling as they did. In face of the evidence that there would be a poor crop that action, I say, was a crime against the producer, and I think an investigation should be held into the operations of those firms. I was in Winnipeg in November, and talking with different members of the exchange I was informed that indications of an increase in price were so apparent in July that three or four of the large firms were allowed to buy their wheat without hedging, and that one firm in particular operated and had a twenty cent profit before it started to hedge its wheat. I was informed that James Richardson and company in January had practically 75 per cent of the wheat west of the lakes. Mr. Murray has stated in the report I have here that he set out to sell before the end of the year all the wheat remaining from the 1935 crop. He accomplished that purpose, and it will be noted that he states, on page 5 of the report, that they took a final loss of 811,858,000. Therefore the wheat on which they made this splendid profit lately, as a result of which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) states $8,000,000 was returned to the treasury, must have been wheat accumulated by Mr. McFarland and not sold before that date.
As regards the 1936 crop, the government's failure to continue the fixed price unless the wheat depreciated below ninety cents really meant the repeal of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and to substantiate that statement I need only refer the house to the fact that the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Mother-31111-94
well)-I am sorry he is not in his place and I trust that he is in better health-in the town of Cupar, and in the presence of three or four hundred farmers, stated that the order in council P.C. 2202 really meant the repeal of that act, and he declared that he was very much disappointed at that action. I have the order in council here and I will read the last paragraph, which is interesting:
The minister therefore recommends that the recommendation of the Canadian Wheat Board be not approved unconditionally but that approval be given only in the event of the closing market price for wheat dropping below ninety cents per bushel.
The wheat board must have made some recommendations, because according to that paragraph of the order in council their recommendation was not to be approved except in the event stated. As I say, that really meant the repeal of the act and it cost the farmers a great deal. I calculate that on the 1935 crop, 150,000,000 bushels and more, they lost ten cents a bushel. At any rate, Mr. Murray says they lost 811,000,000. On the 1936 crop the farmers, not having an opportunity to market through the board, lost twenty cents a bushel, or $25,000,000; and as regards the McFarland wheat, while there was a profit on the late sales the early sales showed a loss of ten cents a bushel, which meant another $20,000,000.
And what about barley and coarse grain? What happened in connection with durum wheat last year was a crime against the producers, because, not being able to put the wheat through the board, they sold it at from eight to ten cents under the price of No. 1 northern in Fort William, and in December it was twenty-five cents a bushel over No. 1 northern. There is a serious loss there. The racket put over in western Canada this year in the marketing of barley is one the whole story of which will never be told. Unquestionably it is the greatest racket ever put over the farmer. There were 20,000,000 bushels of barley, a great deal of it malting barley, that went on the market and the farmer lost at least twenty cents a bushel. The barley was cornered by certain interests in Winnipeg and the price advanced, but the farmer did not get the benefit of it because he had sold it. I have figured a loss to the farmer of between fifty and sixty million dollars altogether in the operations of the board, and its failure to operate for 1936 crop.
The Turgeon commission has been sitting, and there are one or two interesting things I want to refer to in this regard. Let me quote from a report that appeared in a Winnipeg newspaper on January 20:
Turgeon probe hears report of barley marlo "corner."

The Budget-Mr. Perley

Counsel bares alleged "squeeze" of "short interests" during December.
Reports of a "squeeze" of "short interests" in barley on the Winnipeg grain exchange in December last were bared to the Turgeon royal grain commission to-day by M. M. Porter, K.C., Calgary, counsel for the Alberta wheat pool. Examining Henry Gauer, vice-president oi the Winnipeg grain exchange, Mr. Porter said he understood the barley market had been cornered in Winnipeg. . . .
The December barley future on the Winnipeg grain exchange advanced 29 cents in December. .	.	. Mr. Porter said he understood the
"squeeze" resulted from the barley market being cornered and the shorts being forced to make a settlement. "Wasn't one of your subsidiaries interested because of its 'long' position in the barley market?" Mr. Porter asked Mr. Gauer, western manager for James Richardson and Sons, Limited. Mr. Gauer said a subsidiary might have been interested through owning bailey.
He said that possibly the subsidiaries had barley and figured in the corner. The fact ;hat there was a corner in barley is, I submit, a major offence, and it is so regarded in the taws of Canada. It is therefore something that should be investigated. Any government or parliament that would permit such an operation as was carried on last fall in connection with the marketing of barley and durum wheat should be censured, and an inquiry should be started. There should be a thorough investigation to find out where the money went and also to look into the operations of four firms in particular in the Winnipeg grain exchange.
The order in council to which I have referred meant, as I say, the repeal of the act, and against this action on the part of the government many meetings in protest were held throughout western Canada. The farmers and the different municipal organizations met and passed resolutions censuring the government for not continuing the board. To these resolutions the government evidently paid no attention but took the advice of their chief commissioner. I say, therefore, that the welfare of the farmers of western Canada has never been more completely disregarded; never have they been so betrayed or exploited, never have they been so double-crossed and sacrificed as during the last four or five months through the action of the present government in not allowing the wheat board to function so as to try to obtain a fair price for the producer, but turning the flow of grain into the grain exchange. And this is the govern. ment whose leader, when he went west in the campaign of 1935, made the statement that his party had been responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It was he who made that statement in Brandon, and the next day all the western newspapers, the Leader-Post in
tMr. E. E. Perlry.1
particular, came out with large headlines to the effect that the Liberals had been responsible for the act. The claim was made that it was the Liberals who were responsible for the clause giving the board the power to take the farmers' wheat at a fixed minimum price. In fact, the right hon. gentleman claimed credit for practically the whole of the act. I submit that no greater misrepresentation of facts was ever indulged in by any public man in Canada, and in my opinion it was most unfortunate that even the farmers fell for it.
As I said a moment ago, there was widespread protest against the failure of the government to carry on the board. I have here several resolutions passed at the meetings I have referred to. Several meetings were held and the resolutions-a whole stack of them- would take you a day to read. There was one passed recently in the city of Moose Jaw. I read the headline:
Unanimous request for grain board. Want minimum price to cover cost of production.
This resolution was passed at a meeting of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities, and the report is to the effect that when the resolution was proposed at least half of the six hundred delegates present rose to their feet wishing to second it. Here is another headline:
Anger voiced as Gardiner not present.
This meeting was held in Saskatoon and I understand that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was in that city that day. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) called at the meeting, but he would not stay because he had to meet the minister. Here is another headline:
Gardiner plea on wheat said to be evasion.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke to the young Liberals in the city of Regina the following night, and then we find him speaking in the city of Winnipeg to the junior members of the board of trade. I have it on good authority-because I was talking with a man who sat within ten feet of him-that the minister, speaking to these young men, a number of them members of the Winnipeg grain exchange, made the statement that to all intents and purposes we now have an open market. Within the last three or four weeks the minister declared that the wheat had been going on the market in greater volume than previously and, oddly enough in view of the pessimistic statements made, someone had been found to take the hedges. I understand that Mr. Richardson and others were permitted by the bankers to carry their wheat without hedging, the market had been so good. He congratulated the grain ex-

The Budget-Mr. Perley
change for the successful way they had carried on the business of marketing western wheat from the beginning of the season.
Now the gem of all these resolutions, and we have many of them, comes from the constituency of Prince Albert. I have here a few that have been tabled, resolutions and protests sent to the Prime Minister. I understand that he has received many hundreds of these, and I think no better evidence could be produced to show that the farmers of western Canada lack confidence in this government and its leader than to have the Prime Minister stand up himself and read from the hundred or more resolutions that he has received from farmers of western Canada in meetings of that sort. I have here one passed at Watrous by the Watrous business men at a meeting on September 18, going on record as demanding that the federal government implement the following, and then they set out that they want the wheat board to continue, a minimum price set, and so on.
Then we have one from Shellbrook, dated September 9, 1936, which reads:
Therefore we the farmers of the Shellbrook district, which includes Holbein, Sturgeon Valley, Foxdale, Brightholm and Cameo, wish to express our resentment and to register our bitter protest against the actions of the government in failing to comply with our request. . . .
They go on to say that they want a wheat board and a fixed minimum price of $1.15 per bushel. Then the second paragraph says:
Whereas our representative at Ottawa, the Hon. Mackenzie King, is not in sympathy with nor interested in the welfare of the western farmer; therefore be it resolved that we the farmers of Holbein, Sturgeon Valley, Brightholm. Foxdale and Cameo assembled at Shellbrook call on him to resign as our representative.
And further that in future elections we elect a western man to represent us.

Mr. King has noted the representations contained in your communication, and has instructed me to bring them to the attention of the Honourable W. D. Euler, Minister of Trade and Commerce.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before continuing the debate on the budget I should like to express my apprecia-

The Budget-Mr. Hyndman
tion to you and to the acting leader of the government (Mr. Lapointe) for permitting me to call it six o'clock when the preceding speaker had concluded. I still consider myself one of the junior members of the house, and I venture to say that some of the older members, from their own experience, realize that it is rather difficult for a new member to make his first speech here. I should like also to express my regrets at the illness of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). During the past year the hon. gentleman became a resident of my riding, and I can assure the house that we in Carleton county deem it a distinct honour to have such an outstanding Canadian in our midst.
When the budget was delivered in this house I think every hon. member was ready and willing to congratulate the minister on the manner in which he presented it. A statement was made in the very first paragraph, however, with which I can hardly agree. The minister said that if he could not bring brevity, at least he could bring good cheer. As far as financial conditions and trade are concerned perhaps he did bring us some measure of good cheer, but that was not the case in regard to the vital interests of this country.
On this occasion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to address the house on behalf of three groups in this country; that is, the farmers, the unemployed and the taxpayers. After listening very attentively to the budget, and having read it very carefully; having read also the splendid speech delivered a short time ago by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), I have been unable to find anything promising any advantage to the farmers of eastern Canada. When I speak of eastern Canada I mean the farmers from the great lakes down to the maritimes, and in particular the farmers of Carleton county. Right here I should like to state that last summer the farmers of my county had a very, very favourable year. They had good crops; there was no drought, and no difficulties at all as far as the farming situation was concerned. Fortunately the price of barley was high, but that was not due to this government; we must thank providence for that, in a way. That was not the result of the trade agreement between this country and the United States, but it was wholly due to the failure of the corn crop across the border. If the price of barley had not been high last summer the farmers in my own county at least would have suffered very materially.
I should have liked also to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance, if he had been here, to the fact that on the day. he delivered his budget he could have stepped

out of his back door and looked into the faces of 215 families who are on relief. He could have seen also a township belonging to my county which is on the point of bankruptcy.
This evening, Mr. Speaker, I want to divorce myself from any party. For the next forty minutes I am not a Tory, a Liberal, a member of the C.C.F. or of the Social Credit group.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And then you will go back?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I may go back afterwards, but I want to speak about the people among whom I have lived and practised my profession for the past eighteen years. I do not think anyone in this house knows better than I the conditions under which those people live. I should like to make it clear that any figures I quote have been secured from either the bureau of statistics, the Labour Gazette or Hansard, so I assume that they are accurate. First I should like to say a word as to the importance of agriculture. No doubt hon. members have read the last annual statement made by the president of the Imperial Bank of Canada, in which he said that the dollar value of primary production of Canada for 1936 was approximately as follows:
Agriculture, $800,000,900.
Forestry, $250,000,000.
Fisheries, $40,000,000.
Trapping. $8,500,000.
Mining, $370,000,000.
Electric power, $175,000,000.
Those items total SI,643.500,000 and these figures, especially with regard to agriculture, are by no means complete. I should like to point out also that the value in dollars of the agricultural production of Canada in 1936 was far higher than the value of any other production. Therefore I am speaking of an important industry. According to the census of 1931 there were 1,128,154 farmers in Canada, and of these 651,648 were farm owners. The total government revenue from income tax last year amounted to 882,710,000, but the amount paid by farmers was only $46,609.35. In other words, more than a million persons employed in agriculture were able to pay only some $46,000 in income tax.
Last year in this house I brought up the question of the revenue derived from different types of farms, and I may say that this revenue has not increased very much during the past year. I am going to be very brief. One farmer with a 200 acre farm, valued at $9,000, with a herd of 30 cows and shipping milk to the dairy, received an income of $2,151.50, with expenses of $1,640, leaving a net total of Sail.50 with which to keep himself and his family. The price of cheese advanced slightly last year, as was prophesied by the

Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). This having happened, the government cut off the bonus on cheese. Another farmer, shipping his milk to a cheese factory, received $710 from a herd of fourteen cattle. His expenses were $506, which left him $204 for the year. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Matapedia (Mr. Lapointe) say a word this afternoon for the farmers of eastern Canad'a. This summer the United Farmers of Ontario held a meeting, and I should like to quote a report of the remarks of the president and past president, as follows:
"Prospects, therefore, are that in many sections of Ontario the farmer's net proceeds on the year's operations will be far from satisfactory,'' was Mr. Nicholson's conclusion.
"We are pleased to note during the past year, activities on the part of a number of countries leading toward an increase in international trade," he went on. "This is a step in the right direction, but increased trade alone will not solve the problem of the farmer."
The past president, Mr. Amos, is reported as follows:
How can any industry like ours be prosperous and carry on under a debt load up to the total value of the whole agrarian assets of the farmer, whose buildings are deteriorating, his fences falling down and his machinery in disrepair? How can he carry on under these conditions, and how can the morale of the farmer grow in strength? I am sorry to say I cannot see much light ahead.
I feel also that we are not paying enough attention to our home markets. I realize the importance of external markets, but we should not neglect our home markets. I should like to give some figures showing the percentage of consumption in the Canadian market of different commodities. These figures, taken from the Canada Year Book, for 1933-34, are as follows:
