I think these figures show the importance of our home market. The prices received by the farmer of eastern Canada have not increased materially in the past year. In 1935 he received for beef cattle only five cents a pound; in 1936 he received 4J cents a pound, and at the present time he is receiving six cents a pound. These are the prices paid for choice beef. The prices received for pork were eight cents in 1935, eight cents in 1936 and eight cents in 1937. I shall refer again to pork later on. Lamb, seven cents in 1935, ten cents in 1936 and nine cents at
The Budget-Mr. Hyndman
the present time, mutton, four cents in 1935, five cents in 1936 and four cents in 1937. Veal, five cents in 1935, five cents in 1936 and seven cents in 1937. For cheese he received 9J cents per pound in 1936 while last year the price had risen to 13 cents per pound. For cream shipped to the dairies he is receiving forty cents per gallon.
Last fall the price of pork kept dropping until it reached a level of cents per pound. The lowest point was reached just at tax time. Why? I submit that this drop in price can be laid at the doors of the Canadian packers. The packers of this country control the price of farm products. The packers knew that the farmers had their hogs ready for market, that they must dispose of them or they would go overweight, and the price was forced down to 7| cents per pound at which the farmer was forced to sell in order to pay his taxes. After the farmer had sold his pork at that figure, up went the price. The packers of this country have a monopoly of the products of the farm. Forty per cent of the products of the packers are made from vegetable oils, which provide unfair competition to the farmers of this country.
This afternoon the hon. member for Qu-Appelle (Mr. Perley) gave a very outstanding address on behalf of the farmers of western Canada. I hardly think I need say anything on behalf of the farmers of that part of the country. Federal governments-I am referring both to the present and the previous administration-have not helped the eastern farmer to the extent they have the western farmer. Outside of the small bonus on cheese granted by the previous administration, farmers of eastern Canada have received very little assistance. The western wheat grower has received large sums from previous federal governments, and it is proposed to spend a large amount this year for their benefit. Last year $25,181,697.87 was spent on agriculture, of which $17,247,449.38 was spent in western Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr, Gardiner) threw some light upon the money being spent in Saskatchewan, and he is reported on pages 774, 775 and 780 of Hansard of February 11, 1937, as follows:
This brings me down to the period from 1931 to 1936. During the first year, 1931, the government, in its best judgment, and I think the government had the support of all sides of the house in so doing, paid a bonus of five cents a bushel on the wheat grown in the northern part of the three western provinces. That bonus amounted ultimately to somewhere between $12,000,000 and $13,000,000.
And again:
But eventually the notes taken from the farmers were cancelled and the dominion of
The Budget-Mr. Hyndman

Canada to-day is carrying the entire cost of the $10,000,000 that was spent in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan-
And then he continues on another page:
That, added to the other total of $8,715,000 which I mentioned a few moments ago, gives a total of $58,715,000 which has been advanced by the people of Canada towards the maintenance of people in the area of which I have spoken.
And again:
We believe the time has arrived when the Dominion of Canada, looking back at an expenditure of $50,000,000, should at least be prepared to face an expenditure of at least $10,000,000 over a period in order to avoid similar expenditures in the future.
One would almost think it was a game of poker. They had put the $50,000,000 into the pot, and had lost it, and now they are going to spend another $10,000,000 to get the $50,000,000 back. I believe that too much money has been spent in the west. In the past it has been favoured. Years ago they clamoured for railways and were successful in having two railways pass through the western provinces. Branch lines were built all through the country. Elevators were built at Nelson in connection with which millions of dollars were spent. Then the elevator service was changed to Churchill. More money was spent, and railroads were built to connect with those elevators. Now they come here asking for more money.
In the past we heard of the golden west, and I think that is coming true. If we keep on pouring gold into the western provinces we will surely have a golden west. May I add that I have every sympathy with the farmers of western Canada-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You said it that
time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I say to the group who come from western Canada that last summer when the appeal from the west reached my county we sent ten carloads of fruits, vegetables, clothing and one thing and another to the western provinces. I divided the potatoes and other vegetables raised in my own little garden, at home, put them into cars, and sent them out to the west. But I feel they have been getting too much help, and the eastern part of Canada is unable to stand it.
What must be done?-that is a fair question. What will have to be done for the farmers? I maintain Canada will never be prosperous again until the farmer is in a more prosperous condition. He certainly must get some relief from taxation; there is no question about that. He must receive a higher

price for his products. He must have a market for his products, both abroad and at home. He must have cheaper rates of interest, and I am going to repeat what I said last year: I feel the time is coming when there will have to be a moratorium on farm mortgages. At the present time farmers cannot possibly pay off their mortgages at the rates of interest they are paying. They will have to have a breathing space to let them get on their feet. The group to my left will certainly be agreeable to that. So much for the farmers.
Now I come to the other groups I want to talk about, namely, the taxpayers and the unemployed. I believe we have never had any government in the history of Canada which has thrown out so much camouflage and so many smoke screens. We hear what the government has done; but what did they really do? That is the question we must ask ourselves. In connection with the railway question, so far as I can figure out, all they did was to fire the three trustees. They fired Mr. Fullerton, and if they will give me the same pension or retiring allowance they gave him, and permit me to go on with my practice, they can fire me any time. Then they appointed seven directors to carry on the same work.
We have heard a great deal about the Bank of Canada, and how it was going to be controlled by the government. I want to tell you that the man who is controlling the Bank of Canada to-day is none other than Graham Towers. He is the final resort; he is the head man in the bank, and I think that fact was demonstrated not so long ago when an hon. member on this side of the house questioned one of the ministers about contracts in connection with the new bank building to be built on Sparks street. The Minister of Public Works said the matter was not under his control, but that it was totally in the hands of the manager of the Bank of Canada.
In my opinion nothing has been done for the unemployed, and certainly nothing has been done for the taxpayers. True enough, a commission has been appointed, but I need not discuss it at length because the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) did so this afternoon.
May I now make some observations concerning the tax situation in the country? Figures secured from the bureau of statistics show that in March, 1935, the dominion government owed $2,846,110,958; the provinces owed $999,440,241; the municipalities owed $1,469,142,077, making a total grand debt of

The Budget-Mr. Hyndman
$5,314,693,276. Then, we had an indirect debt, in addition to that, of $6,786,869,473. Therefore on dominion debt alone we pay an annual interest charge of $127,075,580. On our provincial and municipal debt we pay $130,000,000, making a grand total of annual interest payments which we as citizens of Canada have to pay of $357,075,580. Taking our population at eleven million, it would work out that each citizen of Canada owes $616.98 -at the present time, and that each citizen owes an annual interest charge of $32.04.
I know that these charges will not affect the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or the leader of this group (Mr. Bennett), but I should like to know how it would affect the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Grant) who has a family of fifteen. At that rate he would owe the country $9,254.70. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) with a family of eleven would owe $6,786.78. The leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Black-more) would owe $6,786.71. I maintain that this will never be paid, even though we have an increase this year of $200 in our indemnity.
I believe the country is overtaxed, and we will never be able to pay the total amount of our taxation. The sooner we forget about it the better. In 1935 the dominion government failed to balance its budget by $113,986,617; the nine provinces failed to balance their budgets by $63,000,000, and four thousand municipalities failed to balance their budgets by $20,500,000, making a grand total deficit in 1935 of $197,486,617. Under those conditions how are we going to be prosperous; how are we going to get along? It has been stated that one day's work in three is taken to pay taxes.
This afternoon we heard that the Prime Minister of this country quoted Shakespeare. I wish to recall a passage from Shakespeare's Merchant of, Venice which deals with the Jew after the trial. When the judge had ordered him to turn over all his property, Shylock said:
You take my house, when you do take the prop
That doth sustain my house; you take my life
When you do take the means whereby I live.
In the present condition of this country that applies to the home owner. You are taking his home by taxing him so hard that he cannot pay the taxes; and I contend you are taking the lives of over a million people in this country when you fail to provide them with work by which they can earn a living.
There is something to which I should like to draw the attention of all parties, especially
the government side and the party to which I belong. This is not intended as a postmortem, but in the 1930 election the Conservatives received 1,909,955 votes, and the Liberals received 1,714,860 votes.

speechtext: Too many.

All other parties received 274,180 votes. But look at the picture of the last election. In 1935 the Conservatives received 1,311,392 votes, the Liberals received 1,955,594 votes, and-let the two major parties take especial note of this-all other parties received 1,139,618 votes,-a tremendous increase during the five years between 1930 and 1935. Another fact to which I direct the government's attention is that the communist vote of 5,685 in 1930 had increased to 31,151, in 1935.
I would also point out that at the present time-I care not for the figures of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), because he is camouflaging the thing-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-there are a million people in Canada unemployed. I should like to know how the minister got his record. I know that so far as my country is concerned, all that was done was to write to the township clerk and ask how many were unemployed. In my little township we have none on relief, but there are a good many unemployed. It is not a fair registration. There are men in this country who are too proud to go on relief, yet they are unemployed. It has been estimated that if the destitute people in this country were to join hands the line would reach from here to Winnipeg. I should like to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) looking out of the window on his way home and confronted with this line of unemployed, and required to shake hands with them all. I do not understand how the government can expect to increase the purchasing power of the people at the present level of wages paid to the working classes in this country. According to the Labour Gazette, August, 1936, employees of construction and trade contractors and sub-contractors, numbering 37,561, received an average wage yearly of $745; employees in cities, towns, villages and municipalities, numbering 49,946, had an average wage of $385; employees of harbour commissions, numbering 1,137 received an average wage of $882. And so on down the list. The weekly cost of a family budget for a family of five, including food, laundry, fuel, light and rent, averaged $16.99, or a total of $883.48 a year. So if we deduct the amount of the average budget from the

The Budget-Mr. Hyndman
highest wage there remains a balance of less than nothing; in fact, the wage worker is in the hole to the extent of $1.48.
President Roosevelt gave the proper definition or test of prosperity. These are his words:
The test of our prosperity is not whether we add more to the abundance of those who have much; it is whether we provide enough for those who have too little.
That certainly covers the question. It may be asked, how is the President of the United States going to alter conditions? He has advocated an expenditure of $5,011,000,000 on a six-year construction plan.
Feb. 3-President Roosevelt transmitted to the United States Congress to-day a national resources committee report recommending a six-year $5,011,090,000 federal construction program.
While I am dealing with this question I should like to report the opinion of the Duke of Windsor, while Prince of Wales:
The depression and economic disturbance have been largely caused by maladjustment of distribution. The potential output is far greater than ever before. If all employable labour were employed for a reasonable number of hours per week, the "world would have at its disposal a volume of commodities and services which would enable the entire population to live on a higher level of comfort and well-being than has ever been contemplated in the rosiest dreams of the social reformer. Our urgent task is to bring consumption and production into a proper real relationship-not a simple, but a quite possible task.
The Minister of Labour states that he is trying to relieve unemployment, but so far as I can figure out, the only thing that he has done is to appoint a commission to look after it. Not so long ago I was honoured with the privilege of presenting certificates to ten pupils of the graduating class of a continuation school in my county. I never felt so sorry in my life as when I gave those students their certificates. They had those certificates, but what were they going to do? So far as I could see, they had an absolutely blank future ahead of them in this country. We have here a house of commons, but I think the name should be changed to C.C.C.-the chamber of commissions and committees. We have a commission for nearly everything, and the expense is simply preposterous. The cost of the employment commission has been mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and this afternoon by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I will not further refer to it, but I will point out that the appointment, as announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of a royal commission to investigate the whole taxation system of Canada will increase to Mr Hyndman.]
five the number of commissions now inquiring into different matters in the dominion. The others are:	the commission investigating
Canadian penitentiaries, the textile commission, the royal commission investigating the grain business, and the royal commission investigating the extent of illegal lobster and smelt fishing in the maritimes. Commissions! We have nothing but commissions. Now we have this wheat inquiry. An agriculture committee was appointed last year and continued its sittings this session. I attended a few times, but I got sick and tired of listening to discussions about wheat. They talked of nothing but wheat. I went home and looked in the dictionary to see if there were such words as oats, barley, pork, beef, eggs or mutton, and I found there were. Yet this committee talks about wheat and nothing else. Then there was the committee that was appointed to inquire into the prices of farm implements. They have been meeting and paying large fees to their lawyers, but as far as I can see they are getting nowhere. Then we have the wheat inquiry, which was mentioned this afternoon.

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time is up.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As representative of Hamilton East, possibly one of the largest industrial constituencies in the dominion, I feel it my duty to take part in this debate on the problem of unemployment. Hamilton, which is a city of diversified industries, is extremely sensitive to the fluctuations of the tariff, and these fluctuations invariably affect the employment situation. The industries in Hamilton have a capitalization of some $260,000,000 and employ about
30,000	hands, paying out in wages some $40,000,000. There is no doubt that the present government was elected to power by the Canadian people for the purpose of solving the unemployment problem, which, as various members have shown, is still with us on at least as large a scale as prior to the election of the present government, if not larger. The government has been in power about sixteen months, and apparently all that it has done towards solving this vital problem is to have appointed a commission, which gathered together considerable data; enacted the home improvement legislation, on the strength of which building is going on to some small extent; and negotiated several treaties, or rather, I should say, burdened the country with several treaties which have adversely affected employment in Canada.
It is strange that a government that was elected by such a huge majority for the

The Budget-Mr. Brown
major purpose of solving the unemployment problem should take pride, not in any efforts made towards its solution, but in the efforts it has mad'e in the direction of international trade, regardless of the effect on employment in Canada. Judging by the remarks made on the government side, they take great pride in the achievement of the Canada-United States trade agreement. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) stated this treaty resulted in a total trade of some $787,000,000 in the year ended January 1, 1936, as compared with $683,000,000 in the year 1935, or an increase of $104,000,000. Excluding commercial gold from the figures for the two years, he states that the trade increase was just over twenty-two per cent; and, calculated on the same basis, exports to the United States were greater by twenty-six per cent, while imports from that country were higher by eighteen per cent.
This does not tell the true story by any means, because the greater proportion of Canada's exports consisted of whisky, nickel and other products, some of which were not affected by the treaty, but which the United States needed because of economic conditions. While our farmers have obtained some immediate benefit from this agreement, past experience shows that this prosperity will be outweighed by corresponding hardships when economic and political changes take place in the United States, as they undoubtedly will. The greater proportion of the United States exports to Canada were manufactured goods, many of which could have been made here, thus absorbing many of our unemployed. Shortly after the treaty was signed, an American concern offered metal-ware for sale in Canada at a price which Canadian firms could not meet. A conservative estimate would show, I believe, that this treaty has put five Americans to work for one Canadian, and has helped in this way to solve the United States unemployment problem instead of Canada's.
The next major achievement of the present government was the alleged Japanese trade settlement. When the former government was in power Japan made certain demands which practically meant throwing open the Canadian market to the cheap-labour goods of that country. There is no question that Japan, with its low scale of wages and its lower standard of living, can undersell Canadian products under ordinary conditions. During the last few years Japan has invaded the Indian field in cotton goods and undersold the products of the factories of India, and it has brought about the closing of many factories in the United States. At the present time,
along with these adverse conditions, the Japanese government is subsidizing shipping and the export trade on a scale never before attempted in any country, with the possible exception of Germany; and with the credits obtained from these exports she is importing nickel, aluminum and other commodities which are of vital importance to her. It is quite true that the statistics for the past year do not show the extent of Japanese inroads into the Canadian market, but since the Japanese trade settlement Japanese factories have been circularizing the wholesalers, jobbers and retailers of Canada, offering goods at prices as low as or lower than those at which our industries can obtain the raw material. For example, a firm in Tokyo has offered pruning shears, in any number, at a price at which the manufacturers of Canada could not even purchase the raw material.
There is one store in Hamilton which for four years refused to buy Japanese goods, but last year in order to meet competition they were compelled to buy them. As one walks through the various stores in any city in the dominion he will notice for sale lighters, electric light bulbs, penknives, and socks, at the most ridiculous prices. Last fall a Japanese firm was taking orders in Ontario for screen wire at a price 20 per cent cheaper than that at which other firms were offering the same goods. I was informed not very long ago of a case in Toronto where a knitted suit came from Japan, the quality of which was so good that the store could afford to unravel the suit and make money on the wool material. Judging from the sale of these articles at prices at which they could not be manufactured in Canada. I do not think the most ardent supporter of the government could find much in this treaty to help Canada's unemployment problem.
The next alleged outstanding achievement of the present government is the new Canada-United Kingdom treaty. The first such treaty was ably negotiated by the present leader of the opposition some years ago, and from it Canada derived exceptional benefits, because it guarded Canadian markets and Canadian workmen. The new treaty is substantially the same as the old, with the exception that the negotiators failed to protect Canadian markets and Canadian workmen. I have here an article written by Douglas Hallam, secretary of the Primary Textile Institute, which states:
Headlines in the press say that in England "textile zones are related," and a press cable says that industrialists at Manchester, Leeds and Bradford find that the textile market in Canada has been substantially enlarged. The
The Budget-Mr. Brown

textile manufacturers in Great Britain are related because there will be more workers employed there in making textiles for sale in Canada, but the reverse side of this is that fewer Canadian workers will be employed making textiles for the home market than at present.
Twice before in my lifetime I have seen the wool cloth industry in Canada practically wiped out by imports from Great Britain driving down production of Canadian wool cloth to 20 per cent of the market. Last year Canadian mills had 60 per cent of the wool market and the British mills 40 per cent. Now the main wool cloth item has been slashed in the present budget by cutting 18 per cent off the ad valorem duty and 29 per cent off the specific duty. There are some fifty cloth mills in Canada to-day. The British cloth mills shipped in 15,334,000 square yards of wool cloth in 1936 over the old rates, what will they ship in over the new rates? In 1936 Great Britain shipped into Canada 5,130,000 pounds of cotton yarn and 73,725,000 square yards of cotton cloth. It is apparent that under the new duties imports will increase.
To sum up, it may be said that taken as a whole the textile schedule in the Canadian tariff as set out in the present budget prorides even less protection to the textile industry in Canada from their main competitor Great Britain, than the schedule in the Dunning budget of May, 1930, and that in view of these reductions it will be of great interest to those paying taxes for unemployment relief to follow the employment figures in the textile industry during the next two or three years. In the fiscal year 1936 the textile imports from Great Britain amounted to $40,594,719 out of total imports of $117,874,822.
My object in dwelling on the results of these three treaties, Mr. Speaker, is to show that in its desire for international trade the government has neglected or ignored the question of employment at home. It is quite true that Canada cannot live unto itself, but I believe that in making any treaty with any country the first consideration should be how it will affect employment at home.
During the course of his speech the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) regretted that the government had not been able to do more in solving the unemployment problem. I would suggest that the minister take a leaf out of the book of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and call together the leaders of industry, inquire as to their needs and, if possible, grant their requirements if they will agree to bring up their staffs to full capacity. If this were done and the further condition imposed that employees should be paid fair living wages, I think we would go a long way towards solving the unemploy-

The Budget-Mr. Graydon
naent problem in this country. This could be placed under the jurisdiction of the tariff board, and in order that the employees might obtain fair treatment, arrangements could be made under which any employee could make application to the board under a pseudonym, and have his complaint dealt with in summary fashion. In this way the government, if it was sincerely anxious to end unemployment, could provide that working men would obtain fair living wages, without any worry as to whether a particular matter was within the jurisdiction of the provincial or the federal government. The leader of the Conservative party gave a great example of that when he raised tariffs after obtaining an agreement from the manufacturers that they would not take advantage of the tariff increases to raise prices.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the country that it is only a few days since parliament voted millions of dollars for the defence of this country. I suggest that we should be prepared for the trade war, which no doubt will reach its peak within the next year or so, with nations such as Japan and Germany, whose industries are subsidized to such an extent that their goods can be sold in Canada below cost, in order to obtain credits so that they may keep up in the armament race that is going on throughout the world.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to one who has occupied a seat in this house for something less than two full sessions, the budget address presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in the first session of this parliament was very thought-provoking. When one considers the situation which was then brought to the attention of the house in a very lucid manner one realizes that our national position presents problems not only for the older generation in Canada, but for the younger people of the country as well. May I say to you, sir, and to the house that I have had some considerable experience with youth organizations of this province, and I believe it is only necessary that the youth of our country understand the problems with which we are faced to have them assume their full share of the responsibility and discharge their duties resulting therefrom. To-day in Canada youth stands ready to bear its share of the burden; it only needs the leadership of governments and men of more mature years, in order to indicate the trail that it must follow.
May I say also that one cannot sit in this house and listen to the national inventory being given by the Minister of Finance year by year without coming to the inevitable and
inescapable conclusion that the best brains and the utmost energy of our people from one end of this country to the other must be applied if the problems with which we are faced are to be solved within a reasonable length of time.
The budget speech this year, Mr. Speaker, continued to paint the national financial and economic picture, and it brought to our attention in a very emphatic manner the exact situation with respect to the affairs of the country. According to the statement of the minister the unmatured funded debt of the country, together with treasury bills outstanding, amounted to about three and a half billion dollars. I wonder if we fully realize what that means. I wonder if we realize that- if we are to continue to fulfil our sacred obligation to pay the debts that some time, somewhere, and by some means, that debt must be discharged by the people of this land. That is a thing which I sometimes believe is not brought before the people forcefully or clearly enough. According to the statement of the minister it will take at least two years for us to reach the point where, in our national bookkeeping system, we actually will have as much income as we are spending year by year.
Taking that as a basis, Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is not unreasonable to assume that even in times of fairly reasonable prosperity in this land, governments may regard as satisfactory a surplus of $50,000,000 a year in the national budget. Beginning with the year 1940, it will take seventy years with annual surpluses of $50,000,000 to wipe out the national debt which has been incurred. It will be said that the interest will be reduced in the meantime and that the acceleration in reduction of principal will be more rapid, but I believe that any decrease in the interest payments brought about by the progressive decrease in our national debt will be more than offset by other contingencies which will inevitably arise during such a long period in the nation's life. Even at the end of that seventy years we would still have the liabilities with respect to our guarantees to railway companies and otherwise. I do not make any pretense at prediction; I only draw this to the attention of the house to show in a clear way the actual financial position of this dominion. The magnitude of the task is one of which I believe we all, especially the newer generation, should be fully seized. We should be prepared to do our share in wiping out within a reasonable time the deficit which this country has incurred in the years gone by and still continues to pile up.
.1498
The Budget-Mr. Graydon

I do not think any hon. member of this house can suggest that since I have taken my seat as the representative for the county of Peel I have attempted to indulge in careless, useless or obstructive criticism of governmental action. My personal views on matters of that kind will not permit me to indulge in that sort of thing. While it is necessary to be stern and severe sometimes in one's criticism in order to salvage for the erection of a new structure, at the same time I think we should realize that all through the dominion, especially among the younger generation, there is a feeling that this business of obstructive criticism must cease if democracy is to survive in this country of ours.
I should like to make just one minor observation with regard to this. It was my misfortune, or perhaps my good fortune, not to be a member of the last parliament, but after reading the pages of Hansard it seems to me to be fairly clear that some of those who now sit in the seats of the mighty- I congratulate them upon their success-did not follow too religiously the policy I have laid down as being the one desirable to follow in circumstances of this kind. Perhaps it is not too much to expect that the sobering effect of office and of being on the treasury benches will be such that we shall never have a repetition of that sort of thing in any parliament of Canada. Perhaps the results of the 1935 election may be taken in some way as an endorsation of that type of conduct in public life. However, I am not convinced that the people of Canada as a whole desire that our parliamentary institutions should be carried on in that fashion.
I desire to go a step further and refer to the riding which I have the honour of representing in this house. As most hon. members know, the county of Peel is predominantly agricultural, but with a substantial industrial development in Brampton, Port Credit and elsewhere. Therefore the new agreement entered into between the Dominion of Canada and the United Kingdom has a special significance and interest for the people of this constituency. Perhaps I might be pardoned for taking great pride in the work of the last administration in opening up markets for and expanding the trade of the agricultural people of Canada. I believe the farmers of Ontario, and of the Dominion of Canada, thoroughly appreciate the work done by the last administration in providing a market for their agricultural products in the United Kingdom. Even though the results of the last election might indicate otherwise, I believe this is true. When Mr. Rhodes, the Minister of Finance in the previous administration, brought down his budget on March 22, 1935, he stated that

the export trade from Canada to the United Kingdom had increased by 52 per cent since 1932. As every one recognized, that increase was attributable to the agreements entered into by our party. I shall be brief, but the particulars of these matters are so important as to warrant repetition. The Canada Year Book shows clearly that in 1935 agricultural and vegetable products to a total value of $127,500,000 were exported to the United Kingdom. This was an increase over the exportations for 1932, before the agreements were entered into, of $29,000,000. This was the increase in the amount which went into the pockets of the agricultural population of this Canada of ours. The year book goes on further with the story. In 1935 the exports from Canada to the United Kingdom of animals and animal products totalled $54,500,000, an advance of $22,000,000 over the 1932 figures.
I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not in his seat this evening. He has been called away on urgent national business, but I want to congratulate him upon having retained for the farmers of this country the sheltered markets which the Conservative party originally got for them. I was always puzzled by the attitude which he and his party took during the last term of parliament. I could not understand why one	with the wisdom of the Prime
Minister, and I say that advisedly, could oppose in any way agreements which meant so much to the farmers of the Dominion of Canada. Yet he did. I congratulate him now, however, upon having done nothing to interfere with the great work started by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who sits in the house this evening. Great men can change their minds and I congratulate the Prime Minister for having changed his when he realized his error. He is a greater man for having done so.
I should like to say a word or two with respect to farmers' export markets. I think the suggestion I have to make in this regard may be of much importance to the government in power. It is one thing to obtain markets for our farmers but it is another thing for the farmers to be able to retain the advantages they have been so given. I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who has shown an interest in the farmers, see to it that no stone is left unturned to provide from time to time those facilities, that encouragement and the necessary technical assistance which will enable them to maintain that position in world markets which has been obtained for them.

The Budget-Mr. Graydon
I trust they may be able to hold that position and steadily improve and utilize it, as do the farmers of New Zealand and Denmark, who hold such a high place in world markets to-day.
Leadership in matters of this kind cannot always come from individual farmers, but reasonable leadership should come from the dominion government. They should make sure that we take up our quotas in the various importing countries so that the farmer may reap for decades to come some real benefit from the agreements.
In the county of Peel we realize the importance of what I have been saying with respect to the encouragement of farmers to make the best of their position in outside markets. Possibly no place in the whole of Canada has a higher quality or a higher testing whole milk trade then the county of Peel, which supplies a large proportion of the whole milk consumed in the large metropolitan area of Toronto. The producers in my constituency have found that to maintain the whole milk market against all competitors in this large metropolitan area they must have clean and sanitary stables, and must follow various other regulations. Quality counts in the sale of agricultural as well as other products.
While we talk about the opening of our markets for our farm products, let us not disregard that greatest, safest and most convenient market which the farmer can have, the home market in Canada. I was surprised, as I am sure most hon. members must have been, to read the statistics showing the great percentage of our agricultural products actually consumed by our own people. I shall not attempt to give the list on an occasion of this kind, but on a great range of agricultural products not more than three per cent of the entire Canadian production is exported, the remainder being consumed at home. In the light of these figures it would seem that the purchasing power of Canada's urban districts is a most important thing for the farmer and must always be a major factor in farm success. Rural people realize more and more the great value of the working man and his family in the suburban and urban centres having a full pay envelope to make purchases of the products of the farmers of Canada. That is a most important factor.
And so I say to the house that while there has been a confusion of figures with respect to our progress so far as the relief of unemployment is concerned, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) having given certain sets of figures and other hon. members other sets, yet through all the maze of differentiation in actual figures it must fairly be conceded that no real or appreciable progress has been made in the relief of this gigantic cancer which is eating into the vitals of our country's constitution. May I say, too, that it is rather a pity and a shame, because last year as I looked into the countenance of the Minister of Labour I could read there high hopes for the success of the great National Employment Commission. I myself was willing to give that commission a trial. But, Mr. Speaker, may I say to you that if a ten per cent betterment is all the commission has accomplished after a year's operations, then we ought to do away with it or get a new one to take its place or, better still, let the Minister of Labour do a real job himself.
There is nothing quite so revolting to me, Mr. Speaker, as to hear great sections of our community, from one end of the country to the other, shouting that we have prosperity back again. No person wants more than I do to see prosperity, but I do say that it is not proper to shout prosperity until almost half a million people in Canada are in a position to sustain themselves by gainful employment. That is the real test of prosperity.
Then there are by the scores of thousands, many of them good friends of mine in my own constituency, who are drawing wages that are less by a long way than the wages considered essential for their reasonable livelihood. So I say that the farmer's best insurance policy for the maintenance of good markets for his products is that the industrial workers of our great cities and towns in the dominion shall have full pay envelopes, so that they may purchase the products of our farms as they require them.
In the town of Brampton, from which I hail, and of which perhaps hon. members may have heard before in the house, there is an uneasiness felt with respect to the provisions of the United Kingdom agreement which lower the tariff on certain goods, and especially is there uneasiness felt with respect to the textile trade. I do not want severely to castigate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) with respect to this, but wish only to say that we have none of the large textile factories in our county. I believe we have none of those against which the minister may have directed his action in lowering duties. However, we have several small factories which are dependent upon a reasonable tariff shelter so that they can market their products at home. I will place on Hansard an illustration of what I mean. I have in mind the manufacture of woollen socks. Formerly there was a 30 per cent duty on socks, and a further duty of 75 cents per dozen

The Budget-Mr. Gray don
pairs coming into this country from the United Kingdom. Now the rate is reduced to 20 per cent ad valorem and 30 cents per dozen pairs. In the n.o.p. item the original tariff rate was 30 per cent ad valorem, plus a specific duty of 75 cents, and the present reduced rates stand at 20 per cent with the specific duty entirely removed. One of the manufacturers has told me that the profit is very often not as much as the actual sheltering margin included in the specific duty.
In the Brampton Knitting Mills there are about 70 employees. Not- long ago the mill owner told me it was expected that with the increase of business he would soon have about 30 more employees to hire. It is now problematical if this will be done. In view of the changes in the items under the agreement I can only hope that, in the light of the competition of the British spinner with his greater production, his greater manufacturing facilities and his lower wage scale, the harm done to our textile firms will be ,ess severe than we anticipate. I am hopeful af this because I am anxious that the labouring class in my constituency shall not find themselves severely dealt with by virtue of any change in tariff arrangements.
We heard some most interesting observations in the presentation of the budget with respect to the inroads being made by vegetable oils coming into Canada, and their effect in competition with the butter fat trade. Perhaps I may be pardoned for saying that the county of Peel is a heavy producer of butter fat. I am sorry the hon. member for Stan-stead (Mr. Davidson) is not in his seat, because as one of the most prominent Jersey breeders in the dominion, he would be able to vouch for the truth of my statement that there is owned and stabled in the county of Peel the famous cow known as Brampton Basilua, the champion butter-fat producing cow in the entire world for all breeds of cattle. I had the honour and privilege-

I am glad that I am not alone in the house in that respect-and I noticed that not once did she in front of her admirers raise her powder puff to her nose or put any rouge on her lips. In view of the interest taken by our people in the county of Peel in butter fat production, I may perhaps be pardoned for having taken up some time in discussing the matter, and suggesting that the government follow the lead of the great republic to the south and guard the butter fat producers of Canada in the same manner as the American government is taking measures to protect the industry in that country.
I have tried to appreciate the manifold problems which face the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in attempting to balance his budget and make an efficient job of financing this country, but I would urge that, with the picture he has painted of improved revenues and returning prosperity, which to a large extent is probably a reflection of world conditions, the one cent tax on sugar which has been in force since 1933 should be removed once and for all. I realize that in 1933, due to the emergency created by world conditions, the government of the time, finding that it was almost impossible to raise enough money through the ordinary channels, resorted to an emergency tax of two cents per pound on sugar. The other day I was looking through Hansard and, noticing the remarks made with respect to that tax by many hon. members who now sit on the government side of the house, I felt sure they could not but agree with me in the statement that, while this tax was reduced in 1934 to one cent per pound, it is now time that the housewives of this country should receive from the government a really practical piece of encouragement and that this particular burden should be removed from shoulders which under present conditions are sometimes least able to bear it.
One of the major influences which prompted me to enter public life-whether the decision was fortunate or unfortunate for myself or for my constituents I am not prepared to say-was the social legislation which was promoted and brought to the house by the Prime Minister of the day. I do not think that this house should be allowed to forget the situation which existed at that time. I

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
desire to make this personal statement, that I was "sold on the idea,." if I may use common parlance, that something should be done with respect to reforming our capitalistic system. I had hoped after coming to the house that the unemployment insurance legislation, the eight-hour day law and the minimum wage legislation would have been upheld by the courts of our land, but the reverse has unfortunately been the case. As I have already urged upon the Minister of Labour upon another occasion this session, I again urge in all seriousness that the working people of this country are anxious that something should be done along the lines of that legislation and that steps should be taken speedily to see to it that the provinces in cooperation with the dominion become a unit in this matter, so that we may have uniform social legislation covering these important reforms from one end of Canada to the other. I appeal to the government to take this into serious consideration, as one of the most important issues before the country. I also suggest that they should press forward in the long and hard fight which is ahead to rid this country of unemployment, and that they should bend every effort to an early amendment of the British North America Act. It may be because I am inexperienced in public life, but I have never been able to see why a man-made piece of legislation should be allowed to stand in the way of and offer almost insuperable difficulties to the solution of some of the most pressing problems which this country is called upon to face. If the government will see to it that these suggestions are acted upon, we may yet be able to usher in a new day for the workingman and his family, and consequent upon that a new era of happiness and prosperity for that other great primary producer, the Canadian farmer.
For the reasons I have given, and others, it is my intention to support the amendment which has been moved by the leader of the opposition.

what about Japan, a country about which there has been so much controversy of late? We imported $4,000,000 of goods from Japan and exported $19,000,000 worth. With Japan's low wages, they gave us almost $5 of a market for every dollar that we gave them. And trade is improving because in 1932, when my right hon. friend was in the heyday of power, our exports to these three countries were $30,000,000 whereas they are now $47,000,000, an evidence of the fact that we are capable of selling to low wage countries because of our superior efficiency and because in some cases we produce different things. We are, therefore, able to sell in low wage countries just as well as we can in countries paying high wages.
But this is not a new doctrine from my right hon. friend, for I find him saying the same thing in 1934. Speaking in the house on January 30, 1934, he said:
Along with other countries, Canada has become a great industrial country. All countries are endeavouring to utilize their raw materials and develop them into finished products. Where a market existed thirty years ago, there is none to-day;

He was still a pessimist in 1934.
-where one existed ten years ago, there is none to-day. We are endeavouring to supply our own wants and other countries are doing the same.
Now what was the situation in 1934? My hon. friend said that where a market existed thirty years ago-that is to say in 1904- there was no market at the time he spoke; yet in 1904 Canada exported $211,000,000 and in 1934 we were exporting $480,000,000. At the bottom of the depression our market was more than twice as great, despite his statement that there was no market at that time. 3ut I ask this question: What would he have jaid if we could have told him then that just three years from that date the export trade of Canada would be double what it was in 1934? And we are still going forward, and the prospect now is that we shall pass the high mark of the last boom within the next few years. Courage, brother; forward! There are great things ahead for Canada. It is not the time for pessimism; it is the time for hope.
But to return to unemployment. I give to my right hon. friend, as I think everyone does, full credit for his efforts to cure unemployment. But with his policies he could not have cured it if he had had the power to pull the stars from their courses. He promised at that time to cure unemployment and I am very glad that he lived to move in this House of Commons a resolution in which he asked others to cure it. He promised to perish in the attempt if he did not cure it.

As he made his speech the other day I could not help realizing that though he had failed to carry out that promise it was no ghost that spoke to us on that occasion. He did not perish unless a return to this house, surrounded by a rather diminished band of sometimes mute and somewhat inglorious Miltons, constitutes the act of perishing. But I could not find fault with the man who, having tried honestly and failed in strenuous times, admitted his failure. My right hon. friend has admitted that he failed and I am glad of that. I am glad, too, that the Minister of Labour the other night admitted that he had not succeeded as well as he would like to have succeeded; for the simple fact is that when a man confronts the difficulties of a problem and sees what it involves and admits them, then we have more hope for him in the future and there is more prospect of his succeeding in accomplishing his task. It is after all only natural that we have dreams of being able to do things that are difficult of achievement, and sometimes we do not succeed.
I wonder if ever a song was sung
But the singer's heart sang sweeter;
I wonder if ever a rhyme was rung But the thought surpassed the metre;
I wonder if ever a sculptor wrought
Till the cold stone echoed his inmost thought;
Or if ever a painter with light and shade The dream of his inmost soul portrayed.
But the question is not who is to blame for unemployment; the question is, What is the remedy for unemployment? The employment commission has its functions and it has succeeded in doing some good work. But after all it is a mopping up operation. Its task is not exactly a searching examination of the problem of unemployment; it is not one of getting down to the bottom and effecting a cure, but rather of trying to remove the debris in an effort to save something from the wreck and put the unemployed to work. If we are to geit at the source of the trouble we must find out the cause, and our approach must be a fundamental one. And what is the cause? I submit that there is one cause and a primary cause, and that is the condition of agriculture as we find it in Canada to-day. And what is the cause of that? Well, it rests largely on this-that beginning with the depression, and for some years prior thereto, the price of manufactured products was high while the price of farm products was relatively low. There was a spread between these two, and that spread rendered it practically impossible for the farmer to attain a decent standard of living

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
and become, a factor in the buying power of the nation. In the year which has just closed, according to the records of the bureau of statistics, 46 per cent of the people of Canada were rural, including some in the rural villages. But with a total national income of over $4,500,000,000 in Canada the revenue of the farmer was $747,000,000. In other words, 46 per cent of the population received one-fifth of the revenue. Is it not well that we should try to get at the bottom of that situation? Our great basic industry cannot live when it employs about 46 per cent of the population and gets one-fifth of the revenue, while 54 per cent of the population get four-fifths of the revenue. There is a fundamental problem, and a problem that the House of Commons ought to face, and face seriously, if it is going to be solved.
Now the result has been that the people have deserted the farms of Ontario. In my own county of Huron between 1901 and 1931 there has been a decline in the agricultural population of 13,000 and in the urban population a decline of 3,000. There is a county certainly among the best in the province of Ontario, yet such is the situation that the men are deserting the farms and moving to the cities. Are your cities prosperous? Look at the relief rolls and see if they are. They are not, and the reason they are not prosperous is the shortage of purchasing power in the country and in the hands of the workers. After all, you must face this fact, that in the cities the cost of production is high, rents are high, land values are high, cost of construction is high, overhead is high, wages are nominally high. If these people were back in the small towns their nominal wage might be lower but their real wage would be higher. I ask the house to consider some attempt to equalize conditions between the towns and the cities, so that we may begin to get rid of unemployment by developing the industry of the towns, and drawing to a certain extent from the surplus which exists in the cities. To my hon. friends who are members for city constituencies I say that it would not necessarily follow that this would result in injury to the cities; far from it. Under the present conditions their burden of taxation is excessively high because of the relief problem, but if the industries moved back to the towns, where costs of production are lower, the result would be to lower the cost of goods; therefore goods could be sold at lower prices to consumers, the market would expand instead of contracting as is taking place under present conditions. I trust that some of my friends here have read-I know some of them must have done so-of the very capable work done by 31111-95
the Brookings Institution of Washington some two or three years ago. With ample funds at their disposal and ample time they analyzed the whole situation as far as the economic life of America is concerned. They studied every form of change in the industrial system which might possibly be considered and then published their work in four volumes. The essence of the story is that the cause of the present unemployment was the failure of prices to fall following the introduction of technical and mechanical improvements in the means of production. That is, prices still remained high. I shall give one illustration; you could apply it to anything you liked. In the old days at home there was a man making shoes in a little village near where I was bom. That man is now keeping a shoe store in an adjacent town. Many a time when I was a boy I watched him making shoes, and talking to that man last summer I asked him:	How
is it that after all the changes which have taken place, with all the fine machinery with which the shoe factories are equipped to-day, with all the improved methods of distribution, when I come to buy a pair of shoes from you to-day they cost more than they did in my boyhood when a man working at the bench made them? If industry is not capable of lowering the price of commodities, then industry has failed in its task. If we can do our work just as efficiently and cheaply by hand labour we might as well go back to hand labour. It is along these lines that the remedy will be found for the problem which confronts us. And while I may laugh at the efforts of the Conservatives to solve this problem, as occasionally I do, because it was somewhat amusing to see them fail after their gorgeous promises, in serious reality we have to try to solve the problem by moving along the lines I have suggested or along some other lines.
I have placed this matter before the house dogmatically, perhaps didactically, because that is the shortest and easiest form of presentation. Do not accept my word for it, but I plead with hon. members; there are these problems which must be solved, and if in the House of Commons we face them instead of trying to scrap with one another there is hope that we may achieve some progress.
I am sorry that the Minister of Finance is not in his seat to-night. But here is one thing that I wish to put before the house; we have heard, and I think all hon. members on both sides of the house are agreed that a policy of easy money is an acceptable policy at the present time. But I point out a difficulty that confronts us when we accept the policy

The Budget-Mr. Deachman

of easy money. When money is cheap the tendency is towards more rapid mechanization, because it makes the investment of money in improvements and machinery and equipment cheaper. That is obvious to any man who has had anything to do with industry. In fact, in our larger business organizations they consider carefully the cost of capital, and, dependent upon the cost of money, they determine whether they will advance still further in mechanical improvements which will reduce labour costs but increase capital and carrying charges. If interest rates are low and, we intensify the speed of mechanization, and if at the same time our tariffs and other obstructions in the way of exchange of commodities are continued, what follows? We throw men out of employment, but the cost of commodities does not fall, so the difficulty is intensified by the very remedy which is adopted. These problems should receive the very careful consideration of the house. I wish the Minister of Labour all speed in his task, for the problem before him is the gravest and most profound that we face in Canada to-day, but I believe that the genius of men who have learned how to whisper around the world and turn a music box into an instrument of art which breathes forth the sweetest sounds, will not fail to find a solution of this problem. If we work with a will and with the penetrating power of thought nothing can stop us.
