I have often listened to the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) and talked to him on one or two occasions, and I came to the conclusion that he was quite impossible, that he would never change. But now I am convinced that if he carries on with the intellectual honesty that he has shown to-night he will soon find it very difficult to sit in the ranks of the Liberal party.
Mr, DEACHMAN: It is the only hope.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can understand his
bitterness, being an exponent of free trade and having to support a party of high tariffs. However, while there is life there is hope.
Last Thursday we listened to a very excellent survey of the financial position of the government of Canada. I am sure that all hon. members will agree that it was a pleasure to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) give his budget speech. It was a piece of work well done, and it is always a .pleasure either to look at or listen to something well done. Then on Tuesday last we listened to the criticism of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). As one who was in the house during the last parliament and

who heard the criticisms offered by the then opposition, it seemed to me that the criticism of the present leader of the opposition was quite justified. In. my opinion his speech also was very excellent, and his criticism worthy and deserved.
The government was criticized for many things, but mainly for its failure to deal with the pressing problem of unemployment. During the time I have sat in this house I have listened to quite a number of speeches from both sides as to who was responsible for the depression. Now the arguments continue as to who is responsible for our so-called prosperity, such as it is. I think the exercise of a small amount of intellectual honesty would be in order in our debates. T have said more than once in this house that neither the Liberal party when it was in office nor the Conservative party when it held office was responsible for the economic conditions that prevailed in this country, in common with nearly all other countries; in fact, I can say in common with all other countries. If our policies improved conditions here, and conditions in other countries also improved, then to be logical we could say that our policies must have been responsible for the improvement that took place elsewhere.
The depression that overtook the world in the fall of 1929 began, as far as Canada was concerned, when the Liberal party was in office. It continued, increasing in severity, during about half the time the Conservative party was in power. Gradual improvement began in the spring of 1933, and that improvement has continued up to the present time. It seems to me, from examining the charts of the progress made in any one of the years since 1933 that it has been almost identical with the progress made in any other of those years. The progress from 1933 to 1934, from 1934 to 1935, or from 1935 to 1936 was just as great as the progress from 1936 to 1937. So what nonsense it is to say that this policy or that was responsible for sudh progress as there has been.
The gradual improvement, as I have said already, began in the spring of 1933 and has continued until the present time. It may continue for some time yet. That time may be long or short, but as surely as we had the last depression we will have another one unless steps are taken very quickly to change the present anti-social character of our production and distribution. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) put his finger on the weak point in our social structure, the difference between agricultural incomes and incomes in the cities. There is no mystery

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
about it. The farmer is unprotected; that is, he is selling in a world market, and he is unorganized. When the price of the commodity he is selling goes down, does he restrict his production? No, he increases it, and still further lowers the price of his commodity. When the market begins to decline in the industrial world the manufacturer restricts his production and keeps up the price of his commodity. The farmer will continue to be in that defenceless position until he has the sense to organize in order to protect himself. Booms and depressions are the inevitable consequence of capitalist production. We are either slowly getting out of a depression or quickly sliding into one; that has been the situation ever since the beginning of the capitalist system, and the time between the period of depression and the period of prosperity is continually becoming shorter.
Now let us see how the depression began to be broken up, or how prosperity began to return. I said that the movement started in the spring of 1933. The first break in the depression, as far as the North American continent was concerned, began with President Roosevelt's first term of office, in the spring of 1933, when he began to pour huge amounts of government credit into various works and projects. Almost every country followed suit, in varying degrees. If you will look at the graphs and charts showing Canada's emergence from the depression, you will see that it, too, began at that time. A phenomenon common to all depressions is that in a period of stagnation stores of supplies become consumed, and again a demand for goods is created. This is occurring at the present time, but the recovery in trade to-day is due largely to government credit and to the increasing expenditure for armaments. That without the slightest doubt accounts for a great deal of Canada's foreign trade. It does not require a great deal of understanding of economics to be able to perceive this fact, but in case some hon. members do not want to take my word for it I should like to quote an authority who I think is beyond question. Sir George Paish, speaking I believe, to the New York section of the American Manufacturers' Association or the American Chamber of Commerce, I am not sure which, as reported in the New York Times of February 7, made this statement:
"The creation of huge amounts of government credits by many nations since 1931 has prevented a complete breakdown of credit and the banking system and led to a general recovery in trade," he said. "The improved trade was due, however, in no small measure to increased expenditure for armaments."
That is a very poor basis on which to build enduring prosperity, and I am afraid it will not be enduring.
There are many points in the budget speech with which I should like to deal, but as unemployment is still the most pressing problem facing this country, and as the amendment deals specifically with unemployment, I shall confine myself largely to that subject. I have already said that unemployment is the most pressing problem facing the people of Canada, but to say that unemployment is the problem is not putting the matter quite correctly. What concerns us, or what should concern us, is the effect of unemployment, calculated in terms of human values. We have not got down to that yet. The previous government undoubtedly was elected on its promise to end unemployment. It failed to do so. It failed to deal effectively with the problem created by unemployment, and for this it was severely criticized by members of the party now in power. I have said before, and I wish to say again, that this government should be in a better position to deal with unemployment than the last government was because it has the experience of the last government, as well as that of every other government in the world to draw upon, and surely it should be able to make use of that experience. I think it is correct to say that the failure of the Conservative government to deal with this matter is why the present government is in office to-day.
During the last few years we have heard a great deal about promises, but I woidd point out that this government has also made promises. I have in my hand a report which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of an address made in Vancouver by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on August 29, 1935. Ten points of Liberal policy are enunciated in this report, number six of which reads:
The immediate abolition of the relief camps, and handling of the unemployment problem on a national basis, utilizing in adequately paid work of social value to the nation, those now unemployed.
I maintain that the government has not kept that promise. I have before me a copy of the agreement entered into between the government of British Columbia and the government of the Dominion of Canada, under the terms of the Unemployment Relief and Assistance Act. I am not going to read all of this agreement, but I should like to quote subsection B of section 1 which refers to the wages to be paid to men placed on farms. The agreement reads:
, The total of all amounts paid by the province to all individuals placed and maintained in employment on farms as aforesaid, who at

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
the time of placement are oyer sixteen years of age, unemployed and without means of support, not in excess of a rate equal, at the end of the aforesaid period to $7.50 per individual.
I understand that these men would be entitled to this $7.50 only if they stayed a full six months. Then they are allowed the magnificent sum of $3 with which to buy winter clothing. How much clothing can a man buy for farm wear in the winter time for $3? How would any hon. member here like to go out and work on a farm in weather such as we have in British Columbia-I admit it is not as cold as in some of the other provinces-in an outfit that could be bought for S3? I am told that sufficient clothing for this sort of work would cost at least $22. This is not putting the unemployed to work at adequate wages.
Speaking the other evening, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) referred to the unemployment camps as being blind alleys. Surely if those camps could be referred to in such terms, this sort of employment is equally blind alley employment. Not only that, but the farmer is to be paid nearly the same amount for keeping the man on the farm. This is not what was promised to the unemployed before the election of 1935. I have in my hand a page from the Vancouver Province of August 1, 1935, containing a report of an address by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). What did he promise the unemployed? The report reads:
Mr. Mackenzie made a frank announcement of his own and his party's intentions if they were placed in power.
There are various things the minister promised the unemployed. The first item he mentioned was the early construction of the First Narrows bridge and. the completion of the Canadian National hotel. I suppose the unemployed were to occupy that hotel when completed. He promised the completion of the Pacific Great Eastern railway to the Peace River or the construction of a highway to that district. He promised the creation of a national park at Garibaldi mountain and the building of the necessary highways. He promised the abolition of the relief camps and the establishment of construction camps to employ men at forty cents per hour for a five day week. He then went on to give his views on finance, which I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) might find interesting, if not useful. The report continues:
Referring to the relief problem, Mr. Mackenzie recommended the establishment of construction camps where men would be given work at $2 a day for a five day week. Under this system, relief costs, including supervision

of work and tools, would be increased by $7,500,600 annually and workers would receive a monthly return, after board and other fees had been deducted, of $30.25.
His statements were cheered lustily by the gathering, but I imagine that all they have up to date is a memory of those cheers. In 1935 the unemployed were not promised farm work at twenty-five cents per day in British Columbia or on the prairies, plus fifty cents per month for winter clothing; they were promised at least $30 per month after board and other charges had been deducted. I remember the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) moving a vote of want of confidence in the last government in the 1935 session for not having dealt with the question of unemployment. The unemployment situation may be slightly improved' now, but the figures in the January issue of the Labour Gazette show higher figures for unemployment and relief in November, 1936, than for November, 1935 or 1934.
The living conditions of large numbers of employed and unemployed are deplorable. In the Montreal Daily Star of March 2 appears a report of a study made of social conditions in that city by various welfare associations. This report is a damning indictment of social conditions in this country. I should like to read, briefly from it:
Unemployment has ravaged the health and shattered the social standards of thousands in Montreal during the past few years, it is shown in a survey completed by the Family Welfare Association yesterday. A study made of all the families helped by the association in January indicates the following:
In every 100 families of unemployed there are:
Thirty cases of more or less permanently disabling illness;
Seven families where lack of clothing prevents the children from going to school;
Nine where overcrowding is serious enough to cause immorality or serious family difficulty;
Twenty-three showing completely lost or badly impaired moral standards;
Fourteen where the children are running wild;
They tell us that socialism would break up the home. The report continues:
Nineteen cases of malnutrition reported by medical authorities. Surveys made by the Catholic Welfare Bureau and the Federation of Jewish Philanthropies at the same time show similar conditions found by these organizations.
Then the report continues:
Unemployment relief is supposed to cover rent, fuel, food, clothing, light and medical care. But the social workers have found that many of the families have practically nothing left in their homes that is usable. During the years on relief the families in many cases have completely worn out all their bedding, their furniture and their cooking utensils.

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
And we are looking for foreign markets! I think we could get a "foreign" market in Montreal.
Another incident reported recently: showed how life on the relief rolls has caused people to change their ways of thinking. The families of a young girl and of a young man had both been on relief for the past five years. The boy twenty-one and the girl twenty hardly knew of another way of living. Since they were in love they decided to get married. Now on the relief rolls there will appear one more husband and wife and two less dependent children. Social workers report that in many families men have given up looking for work and have obviously lost all confidence in themselves and in their ability to work. The development of neurosis appears often. It is found in many cases that even the younger members of a family have lost the ambition to get a steady job and to hold it.
I can truly say that unemployment and its effects are the great problem facing the people of Canada. That problem has not been solved, and it has not even been attacked in the proper way. Again:
In 66 of the 591 unemployed families studied by the association the strain of worry has precipitated situations that in January were threatening to cause the break-up of the home. In 51 others the father actually deserted, leaving his wife and children ineligible for relief. In the one month there were 84 cases of juvenile delinquency, where the children were either involved with the juvenile court or were suffering from deterioration of character and habits which presented serious immediate problems.
Although during January the Family Welfare Association assisted 1,169 families, of these unemployment was a major problem in 591.
Now we will see how unemployment affected these 591:
Among the 591 families the following figures were reported: In 524 the head of the family was unemployed; 201 other adults were unemployed; there were 178 cases of serious and more or less permanent illness-
178 cases out of 591-
-in 40 cases children could not attend school on account of lack of clothing; 47 families were suffering from bad housing conditions; 59 families were seriously overcrowded; 139 families showed a loss of standards; 115 cases of malnutrition had been bad enough to be reported by the medical authorities; 29 cases of mental disease had been reported by the medical authorities.
These conditions prevailed also in the cases reported by the Catholic Welfare Bureau and also by the Jewish Federation. The Frenchspeaking Canadian Federation reported that
3,000	children had dropped out of Catholic schools in the, city since the month of September, because they had not enough clothing to attend the classes.
Can anyone tell me that we are dealing with the problem of unemployment? We have not even begun to study it as yet. While I
have been reading about conditions in the city of Montreal, I believe we can assume that conditions in that city are not materially different from those existing in any other part of the dominion. Some provinces and municipalities undoubtedly have better relief allowances, and no doubt some have even less adequate provision. But it is not only the-unemployed who find themselves in poor circumstances. Many of the employed are receiving less pay than if they were on relief-That is not only my statement, because I can substantiate it by referring to no less an authority than Mr. Arthur B. Purvis, president and managing director of Canadian Industries Limited, and now head of the National Employment Commission of Canada. Speaking to the Canadian Club in Montreal on January 12 he is reported in the Montreal Daily-Herald as follows:
The unskilled and semi-skilled worker, representing some 50 per cent of those on relief, can, under prevailing wage rates frequently do better financially on relief than if he is at work.
This startling statement was incorporated in the address of Arthur B. Purvis, president and managing director of Canadian Industries Limited and head of the National Employment Commission to-day when he gave a detailed resume of the progress made by that group before the Canadian Club luncheon.
_ Reduction of the relief rolls, he continued, is commensurate "neither with the improvement in business nor in the employment indices, and relief costs are even less favourable in comparison."
From a Vancouver paper I find that the relief officer in Vancouver makes a similar statement. I read:
Mr. W. R. Bone, city relief officer, supporting appeal of Vancouver Welfare Federation for $350,000, an increase of $30,000 over estimates of 1935, to meet increasing needs of distressed families:	"It has been unofficially
estimated that a proportion of our citizens equal in number to those in receipt of relief, are maintaining themselves and their dependents on incomes no greater, and in some cases less, than the relief allowances to which their family units would be entitled."
Mr. Purvis referred to the other accomplishments of the National Employment Commission. He said that a questionnaire for registration in connection with relief had been developed. If the answering of questions in questionnaires could have brought relief to the unemployed, they would have been on easy street long ago. I am told that the applicant for relief in the city of Vancouver has to answer four different sets of questions, the questions in all cases being the same. I suppose the purpose is to see if his condition is as he states it to be. I presume
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

the same is true in every other city. The unemployed have been questioned to death. They have almost been turned inside out in order, I suppose, to find out the reasons for unemployment or the causes of it. Something much more substantial and more tangible than questionnaires will be necessary to overcome the problem. What is needed, in order that the people may have a picture of conditions under which the masses are living, is not a questionnaire; what we need is a commission which will investigate the conditions of the people in the country and in the cities, to find out what they have, what they have not, and how they live. Until we find that out we can never have a true picture of how the great mass of the people live. Mr. Purvis referred also to the recommendations made to the government, chief among them being the one which resulted in the home improvement plan which was embodied in a bill that came before this house a few days ago. I am not going to quarrel with the home improvement plan as a palliative. It is nothing more. For, after all, what does it amount to? What is the principle on which it is based? Is it not merely the principle of instalment buying applied to the building and repairing of homes? I have heard statements on a number of occasions in this house and in other places that instalment buying was one of the causes of the depression. I do not know whether that is true, but I am convinced that had it not been for the extent to which instalment buying developed in the boom years of 1927 to 1929 the depression would have come much sooner, though possibly its effect would not have been so great. Through the home improvement plan more money may be put into circulation this year or so long as it remains in operation, but as the loans are paid less money will be available for other purposes, and so we cancel next year and the year after what we have accomplished this year. We are not going to create prosperity by borrowing, no matter for what purposes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In conclusion, I wish to
repeat that unemployment is not a cause; it is an effect. It is the inevitable consequence [DOT]of the system of profit production. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) made this statement:
Profits are the mainspring of economic activity in the system under which we operate.
Then why complain about the logical consequences of a system which we voluntarily

accept? The main concern of the owners of industry under a profit system is not the production of goods and services to meet the needs of the people; it is the creation of profits. To this end all else is sacrificed. Wages are driven down, machines, as the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deach-man) said a few moments ago, are installed, displacing workers; the workers are speeded up; the consequent flow of profits into the hands of a few makes impossible a general distribution of the products of industry to the people who need them. A few have far more purchasing power than they can spend in consumers' goods or than they can invest in productive industry, while the masses lack sufficient purchasing power to keep body and soul together. Those are the inevitable results of the system under which we live. Industry stagnates, workers become unemployed, until during a period of time goods are consumed and the glut in the market disappears. It may happen that in the attempt to find markets abroad the nations of the world begin, as they are doing now, to prepare for war, and then the workers may begin to work again, only to meet the same conditions in a very few years. This has been the story of capitalism and it will continue to be so as long as the production and distribution of the necessities of life are in the hands of gamblers and speculators on the stock exchanges and markets of the world, as they are to-day.
On motion of Mr. Stirling the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Lapointe (Quebec East) the house adjourned at 10.37 p.m.
